items.title: New York Yankees @ San Diego Padres: Carlos Rodón vs. Robbie Ray
items.author: Joshua Diemert
items.content:
Friday night was a tough pill for the Yankees to swallow, losing to the Padres in extra innings after managing to take the lead against arguably the game’s most dominant reliever. With the Rays marching onward atop the AL East, knotting up this series is crucial, and the team will need to quickly move on from that hard loss yesterday. They face yet another left-handed pitcher in Robbie Ray, and counter with a southpaw of their own in a national-broadcast faceoff from San Diego.

Because it’s me, and the Baseball Gods (or just my editors) have it out for me personally, I am once again doomed to cover a Carlos Rodón start. I must once again attempt to reconcile his actual performance on the field, which has been quite good as long as he’s been healthy in 2026, with how unpleasant I find watching him pitch. He’d be on pace for a three-win season if he didn’t have those two IL stints, with a 3.20 ERA and 3.74 FIP that both go just fine with being the No. 4 pitcher in a rotation this deep.

Rodón has gone just 12.2 innings in his three starts since that most recent IL trip, as the team seems committed to making sure recovery is permanent, at least for 2026. In those three outings though, he’s been dynamite from an ERA basis with a 2.84, even if the walks have been a problem. Command is often the last thing to return after injury, and getting the ball in the strike zone will need to be a priority for Carlos today.

Ray, meanwhile, has had a weird year split between the Giants and Padres. He’s suppressed runs well, with a Pi ERA, but he’s put up the second-lowest strikeout rate in a full season of his career as well as a walk rate a point and a half above his career baseline. There’s a bit of a Robbie Ray bubble, and the Yankees could turn around some of their LHP misfortune this year by popping it.

Paul Goldschmidt returns to the top of the lineup and starts at first base today, while Ben Rice moves down to cleanup after his big night on Friday. So-called lefty specialist Amed Rosario will be at second base, but the Yankees have clearly seen the writing on the wall with righty-hitting Ali Sánchez, and will start Austin Wells behind the plate. The hometown(-ish) kid Spencer Jones is back in center as well, with Trent Grisham going on the IL and Jasson Domínguez taking Grisham’s roster spot.

It’s a Yankee game on a weekend, so there’s gotta be one national broadcast in the mix. Tonight’s contest is on FOX.

: Petco Park – San Diego, CA

: WFAN 660/101.9 FM, WADO 1280 – NYY | KWFN 97.3, XEMO 860 – SD

items.title: 'Enric is proving hard to match' - Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe management recognise strength of Vuelta a España leader Mas as Primož Roglič ships more time
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
History continued to repeat itself at the latest summit finish in the Vuelta a España as Primož Roglič once again remained very much in the GC battle, but once again suffered another defeat.

There have been no knock-out blows for the Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe veteran, whose ability to fight back after a very difficult build-up to the Vuelta has been clear time and again on the roads of eastern and now southern Spain.

Yet at the same time, Roglič's chances of taking a fifth Vuelta continued to shrink on the Sierra de la Pandera summit finish. The 36-year-old arguably looked the closest yet to the Slovenian of previous Vuelta's on this latest climb, closing down some late moves and churning out an impressively steady high cadence in classic Roglič style.

But it still wasn't enough to keep Mas in control and once the man from Movistar had received some timely support and a sharp raise of pace from Raúl García Pierna, his teammate originally in the early break, Roglič suddenly lost contact with both Mas and Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM).

Whilst the battle for the stage win was long decided in favour of Marco Brenner (Tudor) and all the time bonuses on the line were already taken too, Roglič still lost 25 seconds to the two other key contenders for the podium.

On the plus side, the riders in fourth and fifth overall, Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost) and Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos) both were distanced by the Slovenian, Carapaz losing six seconds, Onley 50. But when it came to Gall overtaking him to move into second overall, albeit by a scant four seconds, Roglič could do nothing. And thanks to Mas dropping him late on, the Spaniard's overall advantage has risen to its biggest margin yet: 2:10.

"The idea was not to lose time, but we did, which is not what we wanted or hoped for. For now Enric is going very well and Felix been really good today: we'd wanted to be with them and not lose time," Red Bull sports director Patxi Vila told .

"Up to now not it has not been possible to beat Enric, but it's not over until it's over, there's still a long way to go. However, he's very strong, very solid and very hard to beat."

From an outside perspective, it's hard not to imagine that Roglič's very irregular build-up for the Vuelta due to his accident had some considerable effect on how he's tackling the Vuelta. But Vila said that Roglič was not in a bad way. Rather, he'd run into rivals who were racing on a superior level right now. The crunch question, under the circumstances is if he can improve and whether the Slovenian can turn the tables on Mas and Gall in next Thursday's time trial and - above all - by how much.

"For the team the time trial is very important, we've worked a lot on that and we've improved a lot, so we're hoping he'll be able to do it well in the Vuelta a España too," Vila said.

At the same time, on each summit finish, specially in Mas case, the situation was one of recognising that the Movistar leader currently had the edge on Roglič, even if the Red Bull leader was not in poor shape by any means.

"Primož is feeling good, but Enric is a bit better than him on the climbs, and we have to accept that Enric, in particular, is proving very hard to match," Vila said.

"With Felix things a bit more equal, but for now Enric is showing remarkable level of consistency."

The next big mountains challenge is not for another full week, on Friday to Peñas Blancas in southern Andalucia, and Roglič may yet have time to turn things round by then. But on the downside for the Red Bull star, Granada and the end of the Vuelta is looming ever closer, too - and with it, the last chances to capture a fifth, record-breaking, overall title.

items.title: What Alpine got right at Monza and everyone else got wrong
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
The car that's currently sixth in the Formula 1 constructors' championship just took pole position in a straight fight in a dry qualifying session at the Italian Grand Prix.

F1 is used to freak underdog poles in mixed weather, but Pierre Gasly and Alpine's Monza achievement was something very different.

You have to go back to Pastor Maldonado's 2012 Spanish GP pole for Williams (then seventh in the championship) for an equivalent - and even that only happened because Lewis Hamilton's pole-winning McLaren was excluded from qualifying. Which means perhaps the real equivalent is Giancarlo Fisichella's 2009 Belgium pole for Force India (which was on zero points for the season before that race).

So how on earth did it happen?

The answer is really a 50/50 split between things Alpine got right and things the teams that should've beaten it got wrong.

What cost the favourite pole

Mercedes, and more specifically George Russell given team-mate Kimi Antonelli had a sizeable grid penalty, went into qualifying as the clear favourite, with most of Mercedes' rivals expecting Russell to emerge with pole position. 

And it was heading that way after the first Q3 run, with Russell on provisional pole, via a small tow assist on the start/finish straight from Antonelli, who had already made it clear he'd sacrifice his Q3 to help Russell.

But everything went wrong in the preparation for the crucial final lap. Russell was running on track behind Antonelli, however, Antonelli encountered a slowing Max Verstappen at Parabolica and had to back up into Russell, who also had to slow just before opening his flying lap.

Antonelli towed Russell on the start/finish straight, then jumped out of the way before the first chicane, leaving Russell to pick up a tow from Verstappen, albeit closer to him than he'd have liked. Russell called it a "bit of a mess". 

He still improved his laptime on his final run, but he ended up 0.060s behind Gasly - time he likely lost with the sub-optimal preparation. Plus, Russell struggled with his brakes locking like many drivers at Monza.

Russell admitted "It was a very scrappy session" and said the car didn't feel as good as it did in final practice.

It was undoubtedly still a car good enough to secure pole position. Put together Russell's three best sectors and his ideal lap is a 1m21.633s, 0.233s faster than his qualifying lap and 0.155s ahead of Gasly's pole lap.

Gasly in contrast put all of his three best sectors together on his final run.

Ferrari botched it but got away with it

If you contrast how smoothly Alpine ran throughout the three segments, getting Gasly at or near the top of the timesheet from Q1 right through to Q3, with Ferrari's relatively yo-yo performance, you can understand why Hamilton was so frustrated afterwards.

But for Gabriel Bortoleto's Audi oversteering through the middle of the Ascari chicane at the end of Q2, Hamilton wouldn't have even made Q3, and the higher risks taken by Ferrari (and McLaren for that matter) in trying to work both cars towards the front of the grid were more exposed to the ‘essentially sacrifice one car' approaches taken by Alpine, Mercedes and Red Bull.

And the fact Ferrari, even with its updated ADUO 2 engine, still carried a 10-20km/h deficit through every speed trap, suggested properly executed towing and clean laps were even more valuable to Hamilton's and Charles Leclerc's chances.

Considering how close Ferrari came to disaster in Q2, to then have both its cars ultimately (and fortuitously) starting on the second row of the grid is a fantastic outcome from such a messy session.

Monza was never expected to be McLaren territory, but the underlying pace of the MCL40 in qualifying trim was stronger than expected  - certainly far better than its final grid positions of sixth (Oscar Piastri) and eighth (Lando Norris).

"It would be a little bit of a red herring, or an excuse, to say 'oh we have too much drag," said team principal Andrea Stella of the role the car's aero efficiency weakness played. Instead, he pointed firmly in the direction of execution for McLaren's underachievement when it should have been "in the mix for the first couple of rows".

Hidden beneath a solid second and third in Q2 was the first key mistake. Piastri joined the track for his first run at the point where an out-of-synch Liam Lawson was on a quick lap, leading to him impeding the Red Bull in the chicane. A three-place grid penalty was the result, which puts Piastri sixth for tomorrow's race.

In Q3, there were myriad problems. McLaren struggled to position its cars ideally for a slipstream, which was partly owing to its position in the pitlane. This meant Norris didn't have a good slipstream on his first run in Q3. The McLarens were then at the front of the pack for the second run, with Piastri ahead, but when he locked up and cut the first chicane it not only hindered Norris but cost him his tow. Although Norris did improve on that run, it wasn't by anything like it should have been.

That lock-up from Piastri was a consequence of not optimising the outlaps by dealing well with the 4MJ harvest limit that makes it difficult to get temperature into everything before the start of a push lap. On top of that, Stella admitted that "we had some issues managing the battery, and here in Monza every 1% in the battery charge costs you a significant amount of milliseconds".

Red Bull had its own problems

In a way Red Bull made the biggest contribution to Alpine's pole given how much Verstappen's positioning affected the lap with which Russell really should've beaten Gasly.

And Red Bull should have been well placed to pull off some intra-team slipstreaming choreography given Lawson's grid penalties meant his own performance could be pretty much sacrificed to boost Verstappen.

Only if Lawson got to Q3, though. And thanks in large part (but not solely due) to Piastri baulking him in Q2 just as he was being given a reciprocal tow by Verstappen, Lawson wasn't actually there to play the team game when it was needed.

But Verstappen didn't think any of that mattered as much as the unspecified component failure that meant his Red Bull wasn't running at the right ride height for his Q3 runs.

"With how the car was responding in FP3, I didn't think I was fighting for pole, but it was quite a comfortable car to drive for once, and that was actually really nice," said Verstappen, "but unfortunately then we picked up another problem in qualifying."

Which was the diplomatic translation of his "this car is made of paper" radio rant after qualifying only sixth.

It is fair to say that Alpine was as surprised as its rivals about a pole position that it had never even dreamed of before the Italian Grand Prix weekend.

As it tried to piece together the answers on Saturday night as to how it had done it, it became clear that, as much as the big teams had all slipped up in their own ways, Alpine had equally got itself into the perfect position to capitalise by getting everything within its control spot on.

Having a Mercedes engine around Monza certainly helped, as it remains the benchmark power unit.

But one of Alpine's weaknesses earlier in the year – of not enough downforce – may well also have become a strength at Monza because of the low drag benefit.

The A526 appears to be very efficient with good top speed, so that helped lift it into contention.

The upgrades Gasly first got for Zandvoort have also served to give the car a better balance, and throughout practice Alpine had evolved the set-up to get him into a place he was very happy with.

That allowed him to attack the corners under braking (where others were struggling a lot) and take things to the edge through Ascari and Parabolica.

Perhaps most critical of all though was Gasly's perfect slipstream positioning in the train of cars. 

Alpine had confidence to drop to the back of the pack in that final run – as that offered the biggest tow gain.

That is not without risk, because there is a threat of slow traffic ahead meaning you don't get across the line in time (Gasly and Franco Colapinto made it with around 10 seconds to spare), plus a danger of anyone ahead going off and bringing out yellow flags that derail everything.

Despite a couple of cars going down the escape road at Turn 1, Gasly had a clear run and a beautiful slipstream from Hamilton ahead to secure himself the six-hundredths of a second edge that gave him the top spot over Russell.

items.title: The best errors in Yankees’ history
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
Last Sunday, there was quite a hubbub surrounding a catch/no catch call in the Yankees-Red Sox game. Ceddanne Rafaela came very close to making a catch on a Jazz Chisholm Jr. fly ball that then would’ve led to a double play. However, the call on the field was that he trapped it, and that ruling was upheld on replay. A seemingly rattled Red Sox team then gave up five runs in the innings and ended up getting crushed by the Yankees. The victory gave New York the season series over Boston, which could come into play should the teams end up tied after the regular season.

We’ll never truly know how much that call and subsequent replay ruling actually did rattle the Red Sox, but it did get me thinking. I was wondering about the time where a set of mistakes by the other teams proved the costliest. It’s hard to argue against an instance of that happening in a World Series Game 7, so I think this might be it.

Having been down 3-1 in the series, the Yankees won Game 5 and 6 against the Milwaukee Braves to force a winner-take-all finale of the 1958 World Series. The Braves struck first against Don Larsen, with a run scoring on a Wes Covington groundout in the bottom of the first inning.

Braves’ starter Lew Burdette had been the hero when the two teams met in the Fall Classic in 1957. Burdette was the winning pitcher in Games 2, 5, and 7. The last two were both shutouts as Burdette was named Series MVP. This time luck wasn’t quite on his side.

In the top of the second, Yogi Berra led off the inning with a walk. Elston Howard was up next and he laid down a bunt attempt. Milwaukee first baseman Frank Torre — brother future Yankee skipper Joe; Frank famously received a heart transplant during the 1996 World Series — fielded the bunt. However, Torre’s throw to a covering Burdette at first was poor and got away. Howard was safe and Berra ended up at third.

Next up was Yankees’ third baseman Jerry Lumpe. He too hit a soft groundedr to Torre, this one of the unintentional kind. Torre once again fielded it, but this throw to Burdette was also off. A high effort allowed everyone to be safe, loading the bases. The next two batters both hit into outs, but both were good enough to score runs, giving the Yankees a lead that was only partly of their own doing.

Now, those two plays on their own did not win the Yankees the game and the series, but the Bombers never trailed again after that. Larsen got himself into some trouble in the third, eventually making way for Bob Turley. Del Crandall did tie the game for the Braves with a sixth inning homer, but other than that, Turley was excellent, throwing 6.2 innings out of the bullpen, allowing just that one run on two hits.

Turley’s performance eventually allowed the Yankees to breakthrough in the eighth. Howard was involved again, hitting an RBI single to give the Yankees the lead. However, the big play came a couple batters later when Bill Skowron hit a massive three-run homer off Burdette. The Yankees are blessed with many clutch moments throughout history, because for many other teams, that Skowron homer would be the singular best moment in franchise history. Meanwhile, it gets lost in the shuffle a bit for the Yankees.

Obviously, there was quite a bit of crucial moments following Torre’s two errors in the third, but there’s no way to accurately predict what happens if he just makes those plays cleanly. That being said, not only did they lead to two runs immediately after, but that was a bunch more pitches Burdette had to throw in that inning. They probably added a bit of fatigue that the Yankees then took advantage of later on. They may not have been the singular difference, but it’s hard to say they weren’t one.

items.title: Yankees place Trent Grisham on IL with hamstring strain, recall Jasson Domínguez
items.author: Andrew Mearns
items.content:
The Yankees lost in walk-off fashion to San Diego on Friday night, but they might not have played extras had it not been for a misplay that allowed the Padres to score their only run of the initial nine innings. With two outs in the second, Xander Bogaerts got under a pitch from Max Fried on what could charitably be described as a flare to center. It was a ball that most center fielders would’ve at minimum come close to and have the chance for a diving catch.

But for the Yankees, Trent Grisham was in center field, and while he was once an elite defender, he has been far from that in 2026. It didn’t help that he was playing a guy with an 82 OPS+ and only 11 homers far too deep, but regardless, he was clearly not moving well on the play. The ball dipped in with ease and Ty France scored. When the half-inning ended, Grisham spoke to the team trainer and disappeared down the dugout tunnel. Soon, the Yankees announced that Grisham was dealing with discomfort in his right hamstring, the same one that sent him to the IL earlier in 2026. It’s been an uneven year on the whole for Grisham, who has hit .211/.308/.395 with 18 homers but only a 95 OPS+.

Now, we know that Grisham is indeed heading back to the IL. Jasson Domínguez will fly from Scranton to San Diego to rejoin the team and take Grisham’s spot on the roster. The former top prospect had an injury of his own earlier in 2026, but when given the chance to play, he did not acquit himself well, batting just .230/.270/.380 with a 79 OPS+ and exactly 0.0 rWAR.

It might only be a short-term stay for Domínguez since it seems like Aaron Judge is tracking to return to the team soon (though New York has made no announcements) and there’s only so much roster flexibility at the moment. But for now, Domínguez will serve as outfield depth, though Spencer Jones will likely get the lion’s share of time in center with Grisham out. Cody Bellinger is a candidate for some center field time as well, though he did bang himself up a bit on a foul ball last night too.

items.title: 'To be honest, that was not the plan at all' - Kevin Vermaerke follows his instincts in latest long-distance Vuelta a España breakaway move
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Even when he hasn't planned it, Kevin Vermaerke seemingly just can't stop getting into dangerous-looking breakaway moves at this year's Vuelta a España, with the US rider first making it into a huge early attack on stage 14 to Sierra de la Pandera and then making a gutsy long-distance ambush that could have reaped him huge benefits.

A prolonged acceleration by Bahrain Victorious in the chase group shredded his time, though, and Vermaerke, racing all but blind with barely any time references, found himself caught by EF Education-EasyPost's Giro d'Italia stage winner Georg Steinhauser on a steep 'wall' immediately preceding the final climb.

As Vermaerke explained afterwards, he hadn't actually expected to get in the break - his third in as many days following the abandon of UAE leader Tadej Pogačar - and still less actually go on the attack. But once he was off the front, he figured it was best to try to make the most of it and simultaneously provide cover for his teammates in the move behind.

"To be honest, that was not the plan at all," Vermaeke told at the summit of La Pandera, where he finished 19th down after a 121-kilometre breakaway. "I kind of had my eye on tomorrow;, today I didn't want to spend too much energy.

"But I made it into the break let's say fairly easily, it was a pretty big move, and once in there I pretty much sat at back and took it super easy.

"Then they told us over the team radio there was a technical descent coming up. I knew I'm pretty strong on the descent so I went on the front. I didn't take any risks, I just didn't' want to go on a crash and for us to lose another guy.

"So I went at my pace and had a bit of a gap at the bottom, it was a bit of an impulse that I kept it going."

Vermaerke told that under the circumstances and with the idea being that teammate João Almeida, also in the break, could have an easier ride to the final climb if he was ahead, he continued onwards. But then the gap continued to rise and at one point it looked as if he might get enough time to win for himself.

"That crossed my mind once or twice, but to be honest I didn't know the gaps, I heard 1:45 once but that was the only gap I ever heard", he recounted.

"Then when Steinhauser came across on a little ramp before the main climb, it, caught me by surprise, I didn't even know the situation behind.

"I just focussed on pacing myself because I knew I'd need more than two minutes for the climb. So I just gave it a shot."

Vermaerke's move did not work out, then, but his courageous effort kept UAE in the thick of the action once again.

What's more, UAE's placing three of their four remaining riders in the race in the break of the day was the latest reminder that even after the colossal setback that Pogačar's abandon represented, the squad is determined to fight on to take whatever they can in this year's Vuelta a España.

items.title: From 99th to first – Marco Brenner bounces back from crashes and sickness to take Tudor's first Grand Tour stage victory, a result he 'always knew' he was capable of
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
After bringing Tudor Pro Cycling and himself a maiden Grand Tour stage win at the Vuelta a España, Marco Brenner admitted that he "always knew" he was capable of results like this; he just needed everything to fall into place.

Brenner had arrived at the start of the Vuelta as one of the young riders threatening to break through fully at the highest level, fresh off the back of his first WorldTour GC victory at the Tour of Poland. He may have had to wait for his body to recover, but it was worth the wait as he added to that success with the biggest win of his career.

"With the victory in Poland, we came here with high expectations, but during the first week I was quite sick; I had quite a strong cold, then I also crashed, unfortunately, and I really had to recover first," said the German in his post-race press conference.

"But today it worked out and was amazing. For sure, so far it's the best part of my career with Poland and now winning a Grand Tour stage."

Brenner would have known the slopes of the final climb, after all, he raced them the last time Sierra de La Pandera's brutal but stunning ascent featured in the Vuelta back in 2022.

While he had shown promise by finishing fifth on a stage to Peñas Blancas, on the day to Pandera two stages later he finished 99th, crossing the line almost 20 minutes after Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost) had won the stage.

Having come through as a top teenage talent, Brenner turned pro with DSM at 19 in 2021, then made his Grand Tour debut at the Vuelta a year later. Asked in his press conference by a German journalist about how the perception was that he'd never quite reached the potential he'd perhaps promised, Brenner burst out laughing.

"I love this question," he said, admitting how assured he was that a day like today would come. "I mean, for me, I always knew that if everything comes together, I can do quite good results.

"I will never be the guy to stand here and say I will win WorldTour races or whatever. First, it was really nice to win in Poland, and also here to win the stage, but I don't think I should put expectations out there; I'm just happy with how it goes.

"Of course I know now – and a lot of people know now – that when everything comes together, I can also win some big races."

Tudor played the 45-man breakaway that went away on stage 14 perfectly, getting three of their best climbers, Brenner, Larry Warbasse and Will Barta, all up the road to play out the final climb.

As several attacks split the leading group, it became clear that Brenner and King of the Mountains leader Santiago Buitrago (Bahrain Victorious) were the strongest climbers, but the battle lasted all the way to the line after 12km of hitting each other with attacks.

Buitrago tried to steal a march under the 1km to go flamme rouge, but Brenner had the kick to respond, despite having just taken his hands off the bars to adjust something. Storming back to the Colombian's wheel, Brenner took the lead into the twisty corners of the finale, and surged to the line for victory, still with enough wherewithal to do up his jersey and delight his sponsors.

"Today we started, and we knew there was a good chance that it would be a breakaway day. The team was also saying we should try to go in with more of the kind of riders who suit the finish, me, Larry and Will, and it was really a perfect scenario with all three of us present," said Brenner.

"Today I felt quite good. The other day in the break I was not really feeling 100%, so I told the team, and they did a really good job to control on the last climb and in the final I could put myself in a position to try and win the race.

"You live for days like today, I guess. There’s not many cyclists who achieve a stage win within a Grand Tour, and to add this to my palmarès is really amazing."

items.title: Checking in on the Yankees’ August additions, one month later
items.author: Andrés Chávez
items.content:
The New York Yankees didn’t really make too much noise before the 2026 trade deadline. They added a slugging first baseman in Luis García Jr., an outfielder in Heliot Ramos, and not much else. They failed to bring in significant additions to the rotation and bullpen, which was ‘addressed’ with cheap free-agent signing Michael Fulmer and waiver claim John Schreiber well after August 3.

For this exercise, let’s focus on the major trades, namely García and Ramos, and a third player who was called up from Triple-A Scranton but has been, essentially and for all intents and purposes, a post-deadline acquisition: shortstop George Lombard Jr.

The lefty slugger has been the best player the Bombers acquired at or around the trade deadline. The 26-year-old masher started his breakout in the nation’s capital and continued it in the Bronx. He has hit, before Friday’s game, a robust .292/.337/.500 with five home runs and a 132 wRC+ in pinstripes.

García had flirted with above-average power numbers in the past, but he had never put together such a strong season until 2026, making him a bit of a gamble for the Yankees. So far, it’s safe to say it has paid off big-time, as he has given the team a reliable, productive left-handed slugger to plug and play in the middle of the lineup.

During times when the Yanks missed some key power hitters, including the still-absent Aaron Judge, García has proved to be a useful hitter.

While García’s arrival has been a hit, the same can’t be said about Ramos. The outfielder is struggling to the tune of a .141/.286/.266 with a home run, a 27.3 percent strikeout rate, a 61 wRC+, and -0.5 fWAR. He has been with the Yankees for a month, yet he’s already their least valuable position player by fWAR.

If we see Ramos’ performance with the Yankees without context, he has been a disaster. However, it’s important to point out that since August 20, he has been hitting a solid .227/.370/.455 with a homer, two doubles, and a 136 wRC+ in 27 plate appearances. His expected stats also suggest he’s been quite unlucky in New York; he’s got a perfectly solid .338 expected wOBA as a Yankee. See, for instance, the hardest-hit double play ball in the majors this year:

Perhaps if we give him some more time, his overall stat line would look a lot better.

Ramos isn’t much of a defender, and he isn’t particularly fast, either, but in time, he’ll prove that he’s a fine hitter with power. His role will undoubtedly diminish when Aaron Judge returns from injury, though.

The Yankees decided to start the Lombard clock on August 4, right after the deadline. And what a ride it has been. He started his MLB tenure on fire, with highlight-reel defensive plays and two homers in his first four games.

After a few weeks, his offensive performance started to diminish, and he had a .253/.310/.367 line with a 90 wRC+ on Tuesday, when he had to depart a game after injuring his knee. He dodged a bullet and, after missing a few days, returned to the lineup on Friday.

The Yankees are committed to letting him develop at the MLB level. After all, he made light work of Double-A and Triple-A pitchers this year.

Lombard is the Yankees’ shortstop of the future. He’s an extremely young player, and he may make mistakes in bunches, but the potential is there for him to impact games both offensively and defensively (and on the basepaths, too) for a long time.

items.title: How Piastri's Q3 mistake denied Norris "half a second" in Italian GP qualifying
Vuelta a España stage 15 shortened by 70km to protect the health of the riders in extreme heat
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Organisers have shortened stage 15 of the Vuelta a España due to extreme heat, which is forecast across Andalucia on Sunday.

The stage was originally slated to cover a 189.7km route between Palma del Rio and Córdoba, including three classified climbs and 3,500m vertical ascent, but with temperatures of 40ºC forecast for the stage, organisers have amended the route. The distance was cut to just 110.2km, and significantly reduced the amount of climbing.

"The decision was taken following the activation of the Extreme Temperatures Protocol," read a statement from the race organisation. "After a meeting involving representatives of the Commissaires’ Panel, the teams, the riders and the Vuelta management, taking into account all the considerations raised by the different parties and the weather conditions forecast for tomorrow’s stage."

Temperatures throughout Europe have been exceptionally high this summer, with a number of races affected by the weather. In July stage 9 of the Tour de France was shortened due to a red heatwave alert, while spectators were not permitted at stage three due to wildfires in the area. Those wildfires also affected the final stage in Paris, with emergency services required to attend rather be available to police the opening kilometres of the race into the French capital.

While it has been hot for the vast majority of the 14 stages of the Vuelta so far, extreme weather of another sort affected stage 3 two weeks ago, with a severe hail storm battering riders who eventually took shelter in a roadside hotel.

With Sunday's stage much shorter than originally planned, it will start later in the day, rolling out at 2:50 p.m. local time and the flag to signal racing to drop 10 minutes later. The race will follow the original route until kilometre 52, where the riders will turn towards the finish in Cordoba rather than head for the northern loop originally slated.

Enric Mas (Movistar) continues to lead the Vuelta, the Movistar rider finishing alongside podium rival Felix Gall (Decathlon-CMA CGM) on stage 14, which was won by Marco Brenner (Tudor Pro Cycling).

items.title: Winners and losers from Italian Grand Prix F1 qualifying 2026
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
Italian Grand Prix qualifying produced Formula 1’s most surprising dry weather polesitter in over a decade.

But apart from him, there weren’t many in the pitlane with reasons to be cheerful.

Here’s our winners and losers rundown.

Winner: Pierre Gasly and Alpine (1st)

A podium is worth 15 points and a pole is worth 'nothing' - Pierre Gasly has gained a pole and lost a podium in the span of this weekend, and yet it feels like the loss of 15 points is an acceptable trade for his F1 CV.

He's now an F1 winner and an F1 polesitter. That feels right. That feels significant. Regardless of what Sunday brings, he's poleman number 109 in F1's history books.

But it's also a big deal for Alpine, which has felt a bit no man's land-y for much of this season but seems to be squeezing out some good juice from its Zandvoort upgrade.

"I don't think we quite got the best out of the package in Zandvoort. It's a bit of a quirky circuit. But we've come here and the car is responding very well," an elated Steve Nielsen, Alpine's managing director, told Sky. 

"We got the gaps right. We got the tows right. The drivers didn't make a mistake. And laptime's clearly in the car. Because both cars were quite quick."

It's not the first midfield car to star on a low-downforce track, and it won't be the last, but compared to the rest of the season it feels even more significant than it usually would.

Loser: Max Verstappen (6th)

"This car is made out of paper," was a curious Q3 radio message from Max Verstappen, as the Red Bull’s habit of small but costly breakages continued with a problem that affected its ride height. Not ideal for this kerb-heavy circuit.

He felt that was far more significant than losing his slipstream wingman when Liam Lawson was eliminated in Q2 after coming across the slow-moving Oscar Piastri.

Speaking of which…

Loser: Oscar Piastri (3rd but penalised)

On pure qualifying results, Piastri was a ‘winner’ category candidate. Third on the grid at a track not great for the draggy McLaren, a long way ahead of team-mate Lando Norris and all despite (but also partly because of) blowing his last qualifying lap with a trip over the first chicane.

But already by that time a penalty was highly likely given Piastri’s inadvertent but massive block on Lawson in the middle of the first chicane in Q2. And, as referenced above, that Q3 error blew the lap on which he was supposed to be giving Norris a helpful tow.

So as third on the grid becomes sixth, that error and messing up the team’s plans means Piastri ends up in the Loser list instead.

Winner: Kimi Antonelli (7th)

Given the championship leader spent all of Monza qualifying as team-mate Russell's tow servant, seventh in the actual results via one tow-less out of sequence solo lap that didn't matter was quite an achievement.

And one that probably suggests a) he'd have been a clear polesitter if he'd participated in qualifying properly and b) he has a shot at a very, very good result even from the back of the grid on Sunday.

One of his title rivals being beaten to pole by an Alpine and the other only qualifying fifth behind his team-mate and hinting at Ferrari team prioritisation angst already is quite good for Antonelli too on a weekend where he has nothing to lose.

Loser: Liam Lawson (14th)

Best-laid plans, and all that.

Red Bull hoped to use Lawson, faced as we now know with back-of-the-grid engine penalties, to tow Verstappen around in Q3. "But obviously you need to get there to be able to do it," reflected Lawson after his elimination, in 14th, in Q2.

That was much calmer than he'd been on the radio during the session. "Dude, what the f***?" he exclaimed as he was baulked by Piastri at the first chicane, which earned the McLaren driver a grid penalty, before telling Red Bull at the end of Q2: "Bro, that's actually appalling. I can't believe how badly you just left me out to f***ing dry!"

Maybe the Piastri block is what stopped him progressing. Maybe it wasn't; Lawson was three tenths away in the end, didn't improve in the final sector, and generally looked borderline - not helped by the fact he'd "spent the whole quali in clean air until that last lap".

"It was the first time I'd sat behind a car and the tyres were super hot," he said. "It just wasn't an ideal situation, so trying to do it for the first time was not ideal. But I think obviously having Oscar in Turn 1 probably hurt more than anything."

Whatever the cause(s), Lawson should really have been in the final part of qualifying.

Winner: Ollie Bearman (12th)

Having spent the last four months sliding backwards, Haas needed the upgrade it brought to Monza to show something encouraging.

So for Bearman to declare it "night-and-day different" and feel he had a shot at Q3 as he produced his best qualifying result since Shanghai in March will do nicely.

Bearman was also seven tenths of a second faster than team-mate Esteban Ocon. Only Bearman has the upgraded Ferrari engine, but he felt that was only a marginal difference and that he'd still have been fighting to get out of Q1 if that was the only change on the car for Monza.

Ocon has the same aero upgrades. Asked if they worked, he replied: "They worked on Ollie’s side".

Loser: Yuki Tsunoda (17th)

Tsunoda lost a lot of laptime on the straights and sounded totally bewildered by it, in comments that will sound familiar to anyone who's heard drivers up and down the grid speak about single-lap deployment and optimisation and all that jazz across 2026.

"I mean, if you look at the first sector, I was like seven tenths off - and there's only two corners," he mused. "I don't think I've done anything massively wrong, enough to lose a lot of laptime a lot in basically a straight line.

"I've done a lot of things in practice and it didn't happen like this."

His grid position is far from horrific - but, given that all of this is obviously part of a mission to prove his value to prospective F1 employers down the line, he's unlucky that what will surely be a short stand-in stint includes an energy-starved track like this, whether either a lack of experience with these cars' quirks or a freak deployment issue or both can really, really bite.

Winner: Valtteri Bottas (19th)

"It seems like we're on a better run. Things are working as they should. Like I said, it's also easy to find the rhythm when you can actually get laps with a car that works."

Bottas was talking about the execution of the weekend so far for his side of the Cadillac garage - "not really a single issue" - but his comments may as well apply to the wider picture of his season.

He's on a 6-0 run versus team-mate Sergio Perez in qualifyings, a significant reversal after a start to the season shaky enough on paper to where people started talking about potential replacements for 2027.

Perez had some issues through Q1 and didn't get the tow he would've liked - but also acknowledged Bottas put in a strong effort he "couldn't match".

For tomorrow, both still need to get through the opening stint - with Bottas worried about how the brakes will cope with running in traffic - but amid those continued teething problems for Cadillac things have certainly trended right for Bottas.

Loser: Aston Martin (21st + 22nd)

After the measured optimism the previous two rounds have offered, the Italian GP weekend has been a bruising reality check for Aston Martin-Honda so far.

OK, Fernando Alonso might've outqualified the two Cadillacs (and therefore possibly Alex Albon's Williams) had he made it out for a second run in Q1. Alonso certainly felt there was more laptime to come.

"We only did one set of tyres and the time we set was done with a scrubbed set, after waiting on the pitlane for a long time, cold tyres, etc.," he said. "So I think there was something more to come on the last attempt."

But the reason he didn't get to exploit it, and had to hop out of the car early before Q1 had ended? "The engine didn't start, so we had a problem with the power unit. I don't know if it's the ICE power or the battery or whatever it is, but yeah, it didn't start."

Sunday could be a long, lonely afternoon.

items.title: 'Today's time gap was thanks to Raúl' - Vuelta a España leader Enric Mas pays tribute to teammate García Pierna for distancing key rival Primož Roglič
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Just as on the stage to Calar Alto two days earlier, Mas' teammate Raúl García Pierna had made it into the early break, and once again the two joined forces at a crucial moment in the stage.

With less than two kilometres to go, when García Pierna opened up the throttle, Mas could follow, as could Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) while Roglič - previously seeming much stronger than he had done on the Calar Alto climb and only slightly distanced - could not respond.

Those gaps remained in place all the way to the line, with the result that Mas could claim another 25 seconds, and Roglič, now 2:10 down on the Vuelta leader, dropped to third overall, behind Gall.

Even if Mas did not manage to show the same kind of climbing superiority that he has done in Aitana or Calar Alto, then, the end result was what counts and once again the momentum remained with the race leader. Roglič has not been dealt a decisive blow but it was no surprise that Mas was in an ebullient mood afterwards, particularly as Sierra de la Pandera was where he lost around 30 seconds to the Slovenian back in 2022. This time, the boot remained on the other foot.

"It's true that today's time gap was thanks to Raúl but really the whole team has helped," Mas said, with Ivan Romeo in particularly once again working exceptionally hard for him again on the lower slopes of the crucial climb.

"These kinds of gaps calm me down, because it was very important to gain more time, and today we really did benefit from that.

"I put in a couple of attacks, but it was more to test my rivals than anything else, and see how they responded."

Asked specificaly how García Pierna and he had managed to drop Roglič, Mas joked that, "Raúl went so hard that he almost dropped me. It was a key moment that allowed me to get that time gap".

"One of them worked out, and that was it. I just have to thank the whole team for the work they did.

"I have bad memories of this climb, Primož got nearly half a minute on me back in 2022 here, so the contrast is a big one, and fortunately in my favour."

Mas will now face the next three much easier stages and the second rest day on Monday feeling calmer given he now has an advantage that is continuing to increase on each mountain stage. But if he recognised at one point after the stage, that he "was keen to win the Vuelta", Mas was in no way taking for granted that he could be sure of the final victory, even with a bigger lead than 24 hours earlier.

"There's still more than one week to go, anything can happen, but for now I'm enjoying being in the red jersey," Mas concluded. "I have to be happy and proud at the end of it all."

items.title: 'I didn't want to take too much risk with the heat' – Felix Gall moves past Primož Roglič into second at Vuelta a España but feels the exhaustion building
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Despite feeling the unbearable heat of southern Spain in September, Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) moved up to second overall at the Vuelta a España on stage 14, gaining 25 seconds on Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) with a late move to overtake the former four-time winner.

While Gall's team had previously been the aggressors for much of this Vuelta, the Austrian admitted post-race that he approached the final, brutal climb to Sierra de La Pandera with more caution due to the extreme heat in recent days, worried about the fatigue build-up towards the end of the second week.

After Movistar controlled all day, he made a few accelerations on the steeper slopes, but was always unable to distance race leader Enric Mas (Movistar), who had Raul Garcia Pierna for help before Gall made a final push to the line, again unable to find separation from the Spaniard. But he was more than happy to have left fellow podium contenders Roglič and Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost) behind in the last 2km.

"I guess in a Grand Tour, end of week two, you never really know how good you are; you don't feel so good, and then when it counts, the legs are there. That's the most important," Gall told reporters at the finish on Saturday.

"Movistar made it pretty hard in the final. I think I didn't want to take too much risk with the heat of the last days and also today again, so I wanted to wait and see how I would feel and wait until the end, and I'm super happy I could gain a few seconds in the final and that the shape is there."

For Gall, his second place is virtually still third if you take into account the expected advantage Roglič has over him in time trialling, with the 32km flat race against the clock likely to see his four-second advantage extinguished by the Slovenian.

But it's another sign of his form improving, or at least the fatigue accumulation impacting all of his rivals, bar Mas, more than him for the moment. He knew he had to gain time before the time trial to give himself the best chance of securing the podium, and potentially second – the result which he managed at the Giro d'Italia earlier this season behind Jonas Vingegaard.

Asked if he was in fact getting better as the days go on, Gall said, "I mean it's hard to say; fatigue is for sure building up, also with the heat it's just really exhausting. Yeah, obviously it's going well, and I'm happy.

"[A podium finish] is what we came here for, and that's still the same goal. Today was important to gain a few seconds ahead of the TT, which is the next GC day. After that, we only have two – well, not only – it's still a super hard week to go, but then two hard mountain stages to go, so it was important today to still gain some time."

Gall remains 2:06 from the lead of Mas, which isn't insurmountable, but will require the performance of his life on those final two mountain days he speaks of if he wants to snatch red from the home favourite.

He needs to survive through the next three flatter stages, get through the time trial within striking distance, then use stage 19's summit finish to Peñas Blancas (18.8km at 6.5%) next Friday as his first opportunity to take time back, either on Mas or the likes of Roglič, if he really slipped away in the race against the clock.

Perhaps the best thing working in the Austrian's favour, however, is just how brutal the penultimate stage to Collado del Alguacil is, with the narrow, poorly-surfaced, and viciously-steep hors categorie climb in Sierra Nevada arriving at the end of a brutal day with 4,900 metres of elevation gain.

items.title: Hamilton's obvious frustration at Ferrari team tactics
items.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
items.content:
Lewis Hamilton believes his Ferrari Formula 1 team is putting its "dimming" chances of a 2026 title comeback at risk by not prioritising his campaign over team-mate Charles Leclerc's.

Hamilton trails championship leader Kimi Antonelli - who is starting at the back at Monza due to engine penalties - by 59 points and has 28 in hand over Leclerc.

He already felt last time out at Zandvoort that Ferrari's race execution didn't do enough to prioritise him as the driver ahead in the championship - contrasting it to how Mercedes played its cards with Antonelli and George Russell - and in qualifying at Monza saw another example of what he clearly sees as Ferrari leaving opportunities on the table.

There were a lot of knowing pauses as Hamilton recounted his session - in which he ultimately placed fifth, one spot behind Leclerc - and emphasised the importance of teamwork and the size of the deficit to Antonelli.

"I mean, we're at a point in the year where 59 points is a huge - huge - deficit to recover from, especially when Mercedes continue to be the leaders in speed. So yeah, we do have to work as a team," he mused, before making his feelings clear with a couple of half-finished sentences: "Have we been...  if and when that would ever change... We'll find out, but all I can do is just try to arrive and do the best job I can."

Unrelated to the championship position, Hamilton has priority this weekend in terms of when he runs in qualifying relative to Leclerc - and naturally chose to go behind his team-mate, with slipstream more valuable here than at any other track.

Leclerc acknowledged this already on Thursday - but also said he didn't expect Ferrari to "compromise" his qualifying because of this, and indicated he would be happy to tow Hamilton along while himself having a rival car to get a slipstream from.

This appeared to be at the heart of what got Hamilton talking about championship position and priority on Saturday.

Though happy with his Ferrari, Hamilton was very close to missing the Q3 cut entirely - just 0.001s up on 11th-placed Gabriel Bortoleto in the end - and indicated his Q2 session was hindered by Leclerc's run plan preferences.

"We were supposed to do a push-cool-cool-push. But because everyone was waiting and Charles didn't want to go out first, we had to wait-wait-wait. And then we only got one push. And, yeah, it made it pretty challenging for us," he explained.

Q3 was then operationally suboptimal - he was supposed to be right behind Leclerc on both runs, but Ferrari didn't send him out early enough on run one - leaving him to run all by himself, a good third of the lap behind most of the grid.

"I didn't have any wheels on the car basically and everyone left whilst my engine was running.

"And that just put me out of rhythm [for the second run] because when you're following another car, when you're in that tow, you arrive much faster so the braking zones are different. And then when you're on your own, you lose the tows. A lot of time lost in the tows."

Asked about the conversations that have happened since Zandvoort in terms of teamwork and strategy, given his unhappiness there, Hamilton paused for a while - and didn't really answer the question in the end.

"What I can say is, Pierre [Gasly] did a great job of… clearly, looking from a distance, it looked like they [Alpine] worked really well as a team."

Asked by The Race whether Ferrari needs to throw its weight behind the lead driver given there remains a sniff of the title, he said: "There's light at the end of the tunnel, but it's getting dimmer the further we get through. Even though the team's doing an amazing job in bringing upgrades and pushing us forward, I'm so proud of everyone working- I say it all the time, but it's because I really am. I couldn't do what I do without seeing the great work of everybody, and I feel like I always want to make sure that I acknowledge them and recognise them for that, because I want them to continue to push and I want them to stay hungry and keep that passion and fire. 

"But also at the track, we need to come correct and act accordingly to make sure we get the result we need."

The issue, however, remains the same for Ferrari, which has Leclerc on an even longer-term contract now and would strain to make the case to the Monegasque that it's already time to give up on his title hopes in favour of Hamilton's.

A total of 283 points should remain up for grabs in F1 this season, which Leclerc can argue should be sufficient for him to stay in the hunt, too - especially as he and Hamilton have been virtually indistinguishable in terms of the qualifying head-to-head this year.

items.title: Piastri gets grid penalty for Lawson Q2 incident
items.author: Jon Noble
items.content:
Oscar Piastri has lost third-place on the grid for Formula 1’s Italian Grand Prix after impeding Liam Lawson in qualifying.

Towards the end of Q2, the McLaren driver exited the pits on an out-lap just as the Red Bull duo of Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson were beginning their final push laps.

The Red Bulls were running out of sync with the field as Lawson had towed Verstappen initially and Verstappen was trying to help Lawson get through to Q3 by returning the favour.

Piastri managed to get out of the way of Verstappen, but as Piastri turned into the first chicane he baulked Lawson, who lost valuable time that he was unable to recover later in the lap.

Piastri was summoned to see the stewards after qualifying, and explained that while had been warned about the Red Bull duo approaching, he was not aware they were on push laps.

When he realised that Verstappen was indeed going for a time, he got out of the way as best he could.

However, due to his positioning, he had no choice but to continue to roll into the chicane where he impeded Lawson.

Although the stewards accepted that Piastri had been left in a tricky spot, they felt that there was no option but to serve him with a penalty for blocking a rival.

A statement issued by the FIA said: “The Stewards accept that with the information he had, and the situation he was placed in, the driver of Car 81 had, at this stage, no other options available and hence, inadvertently, and also unnecessarily, impeded Car 30.

“Therefore the standard penalty of a drop of 3 grid positions is imposed.”

The penalty drops Piastri from third down to sixth, and means that Ferrari duo Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton will move up to the second row behind Pierre Gasly and George Russell.

Lawson’s failure to get through to Q3 meant that Verstappen was left alone to try to find a slipstream, with the team having hoped that Lawson could act as support in helping give his team-mate a tow thanks to the engine change penalty that puts him to the back of the grid for Sunday's race.

items.title: In praise of the high number
items.author: Joshua Diemert
items.content:
I’m a personal believer in wearing the lowest possible number as a player. No infielder should have a number greater than 25, and 25 should only be worn by a first baseman. Numbers in the 30s and 40s are for pitchers, and your outfielders fill out the rest. That is the Way Baseball Numbers Should Work.

Of course, the Yankees have retired 21 numbers, every single one-digit, and 15 of those 21 are below #25 — yes, I’m finally correctly counting Whitey Ford, who I always forget when listing off the retirees by memory. Add that to the 25 other guys that are on the present roster, when you get added to the big-league club there aren’t that many options to put on your back. In 2016, Aaron Judge ran into this problem, eventually deciding to keep the #99 issued to him in spring training. That #99 will likely be the next number the Yankees retire, and I think it’s a part of what’s made him one of the faces of baseball over the past decade.

Now we have a pair of rookies filling out the middle of the Yankee order, both of them sporting unusual jersey numbers for much the same reason that Judge did. George Lombard Jr. is #96 and Spencer Jones #78, George one of three MLB players to sport those digits this year and one of them was Quad-A relief depth Yovanny Cruz for these same Yankees. Jones wears a slightly more popular number, even if I only know one of the other guys who share 78:

And despite my penchant for lower numbers (I’m #24 myself), I love what Lombard and Jones have done, even if it was by accident. It’s difficult to stand out on the current Yankee roster — ok, it’s difficult to stand out on what the ideal current Yankee roster is. Even if you’re a threeish win player, pretty good, you’re going to end up behind the big three in the rotation, Cody Bellinger, Ben Rice, Jazz Chisholm Jr. and of course the captain himself. This goes triple when you try and stand out in the annals of Yankee history itself.

#78 and 96 allow the youngsters to carve out a bit of their own identity, just a little. It probably isn’t going to last. Ben Rice was issued #93 for his first taste of MLB in 2024, and once he carved out a permanent role for himself on the team switched to the much more sensible, and aesthetically pleasing, #22. If Jazz doesn’t return to the team this winter, #13 becomes an obvious option for George if he can stick to the roster, ditto for #12 if the club lets Trent Grisham walk. #78 is a little more of a reasonable number albeit one more for relievers than starting centerfielders, but it wouldn’t be surprising to see Jones switch down as well.

With a club as numerically complicated as the Yankees, picking something a little funky and unconventional makes me like you just a little more — indeed, perhaps more than GLJ’s current performance deserves. We’ve seen how Judge has been able to take a strange jersey assignment and make it his own. I’m not asking either Spencer or George to be Aaron Judge, just to want to be as much of an individual in an org that sometimes squashes that.

items.title: Vuelta a España: Marco Brenner fires searing acceleration on final corners of Sierra de la Pandera summit finish for stage 14 win
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Marco Brenner (Tudor Pro Cycling) overcame the stifling head of the Andalucian mountains to win stage 14 of the Vuelta a España on Saturday.

Brenner had been part of a huge, 45-man breakaway group which had escaped early in the day, and which had been allowed to compete for the stage by the peloton on a brutal day. As the group was whittled down on the final climb, a four-man group came together, the eventually German following a move by Santiago Buitrago (Bahrain Victorious) in the final kilometre.

Buitrago came home second, consolidating his lead in the mountains classification, while Cristián Rodríguez (XDS Astana) was third.

In the peloton, the final climb proved decisive, with Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-hansgrohe) gapped in the final two kilometres, losing time to Felix Gall (Decathlon-CMA CGM) and race leader Enric Mas (Movistar).

Mas continues to lead the race overall, 2:06 ahead of Gall, who moved head of Roglič, who lost 15 seconds on the day.

Brenner’s victory was only his second WorldTour win, coming hot on the heels of his GC victory at the Tour de Pologne last month. It was also the first Grand Tour stage win for the Tudor Pro Cycling team.

“I cannot really believe it,” Brenner said. “Until now I was not feeling like myself, and I was struggling with some sickness early in the race and had a crash. But I really wanted to show myself, but also my teammates who have been working really hard for me the whole time that I can be up there.

“Also today I had two guys with me in the breakaway that did a super job. On the final climb I could actually feel that I have the kick, and I felt better and better throughout the day, and in the end I started believing in it.

“I made the move, and Santiago passed me, but I could catch up, and then in the end I could beat him in the sprint.

“There’s not many cyclists who achieve a stage within a Grand Tour, and to add this to my palmarès is really amazing.”

For stage 14, the Vuelta returned to the mountains, remaining in Andalucía for a 154.5km stage between Jaén and Sierra de la Pandera, and with more than 4,100m of vertical ascent the day was sure to be another for the GC riders.

After a lumpy start, the route took the peloton over two second category climbs before the final first category ascent to the line, that final climb averaging 7.5% gradient over its 11.8km.

With the race heading uphill, the attacks came straight from the flag, mountains classification leader Santiago Buitrago (Bahrain Victorious) one of those trying to get away. After a large group went clear on the descent of the day’s first unclassified climb, with 30 frantic kilometres ridden, a huge group of 45 riders finally went clear, building a lead of more than three minutes.

The Puerto de los Villares was the day’s first classified climb, the second category ascent averaging 5.5% over it 10.5km, and by the time the front of the race was halfway up, the Movistar team of race leader Mas had taken time out of a lead which had extended to over five minutes.

Over the top, the peloton trailed what remained of the breakaway by four minutes, but on the descent Kevin Vermaerke (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), the US rider quickly building a lead of over a minute as once again the peloton dropped back.

The second climb of the day, the Puerto de Locubín, began with 30km to go, by which time Vermaerke led by 1:44 with the bunch at 8:10. However, while it seemed the peloton might not take the stage, the American’s grip on the race was less secure, his advantage reduced as he reached the top of the climb.

The Sierra de la Pandera made for a brutal finish to the stage, the 11.8km climb averaging 7.5%, though with some significantly steeper ramps. However, Vermaerke reached the foot of the climb he was caught on the Muro de Valdepeñas de Jaén, a short town centre dig which has featured as a stage finish in earlier editions of the Vuelta.

With Vermaerke dropped, Georg Steinhauser (EF Education-EasyPost) reached the base of the final climb alone, putting time into the chasing group, however, he was caught by Guillaume Martin (Groupama-FDJ United) with just over nine kilometres to go, the pair leading a large chasing group by 50 seconds.

However, they were soon caught by a group of others as the race entered a period of flux, the peloton now 6:30 down.

From the leading group Mario Aparicio (Burgos-Burpellet-BH) attacked, the Spaniard heading into the final 4km leading by 35 seconds from an expanded chase group, though he too was soon caught, Buitrago and Brenner going straight past. Buitrago then tried his luck alone, and when he was brought back, a group of four formed, with Cristián Rodríguez (XDS Astana) and Iván Sosa Kern Pharma).

In the favourites group, EF Education took to the front on the bottom of the final climb, setting a pace and suggesting a move from Richard Carapaz, who won the last time the race visited the finish climb. That move had to wait though, the peloton settling for a little while. Carapaz eventually made his move with around 4km to go, following a move from Mas and heading up the road alone.

It was not to be for the Ecuadorian though, he was eventually brought back by Mas, Felix Gall (Decathlon-CMA CGM) and Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora Hansgrohe), the race’s top four on GC coming together.

It was then Gall’s turn to go it alone, but Mas proved too strong, bringing his move back with Roglič, and when Mas was joined by his Movistar teammate Raúl García Pierna, who had been in the breakaway, the pace he set saw to Roglič’s hopes of gaining time.
