items.title: The worst trades in Knicks history
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
The year-long probe surrounding alleged salary cap manipulation ended on Wednesday and handed down one of the biggest punishments in professional sports history, suspending multiple key officials, fining the organization $30 million, and taking five first-round picks. It’s not entirely unprecedented (see: Joe Smith), but it’s pretty damn startling.

While there are many things to take away from this ruling (particularly with how Kawhi seems to have completely gotten away with this), the biggest thing might just be how unimaginably bad the Kawhi Leonard era went in LA.

To get Leonard to sign with them in 2019, the Clippers had to trade for Paul George, a trade that has gone down as one of the worst in league history due to the sheer magnitude of picks traded and how it kickstarted the Thunder’s contention window by giving them Shai Gilgeous-Alexander.

In seven years, it was disappointment after disappointment, with the highlight being a trip to the 2021 Western Conference Finals that ended in a blowout defeat at home in Game 6. George left and was replaced by James Harden; Harden left, and Leonard is choosing to return to Toronto after burning this franchise to the ground behind him.

In total, with Leonard (likely) going to the Raptors at some point, this is what the Clippers gave up for his services, both to convince him to sign and convince him to stay:

  • 2021 MIA 1st (#18 – Tre Mann)
  • 2022 LAC 1st (#12 – Jalen Williams)
  • 2023 1st Pick Swap (not conveyed)
  • 2024 LAC 1st (#26 – Dillon Jones)
  • 2025 MIA 1st (Lottery Protected, became Thomas Sorber)
  • 2025 1st Pick Swap (Conveyed, Nique Clifford)
  • 2026 LAC 1st (#12 – Aday Mara)
  • 2029 IND 1st (voided by NBA)
  • 2030 LAC 1st (voided by NBA)
  • 2031 LAC 1st (voided by NBA)
  • 2032 LAC 1st (voided by NBA)
  • 2033 LAC 1st (voided by NBA)

This is, hands down, the worst trade in NBA history. It destroyed an entire franchise’s future 10-15 years for three playoff series victories in seven years. At least Billy King only messed up the Nets for five years.

It does get you thinking, though. How bad has it gotten for the Knicks? We can recall some pretty nasty trades from recent or even less recent history, but just how close do they get to the utter franchise-alteringly bad level as the Paul George trade?

Gene Shue To Fort Wayne (April 1956)

Ron SobieGene Shue

We’re starting old school, back when the Pistons were still based in Fort Wayne. Before researching this, I had no clue who these guys were and would be very surprised if we had anyone in our community who’s been around long enough to remember watching them play (prove me wrong if so!)

Shue, the No. 3 overall pick in 1954, was sold to the Knicks just six games into his rookie year, but was nothing more than a regular role player in his near-two years in New York, averaging 9.2 points, 2.9 rebounds, and 2.5 assists in 1955-56.

Very shortly after the season, the 6’2” guard was dealt on draft night to Fort Wayne for Ron Sobie, the No. 7 overall pick. Sobie didn’t do much in four years, playing 191 total games and averaging 8.5 points and 4.1 rebounds before being sold to Minneapolis in December 1959, where he’d play just one more game ever.

As for Shue? He grew into his own as the Pistons moved to Detroit, being named to his first All-Star team in 1958 before getting down-ballot MVP votes over the next several seasons. He eventually grew into a 23-PPG scorer and made First-Team All-NBA in 1960. Five All-Star teams, two top-10 MVP finishes, and two All-NBA selections in six years in Detroit.

The Knicks would actually get a chance to rectify their mistake with Shue, re-acquiring him for Darrall Imhoff before the 1962-63 season, but he started to regress in his age-31 season, and he was out of basketball by the end of 1964.

While Shue never won Detroit a championship, he would’ve been a tremendous help to a Knicks team that went through its first Dark Ages prior to the 70s revival. In the six years with Shue in Detroit, the Knicks had one losing season and won sub-30 games in three of those seasons.

Choosing $4.8 Million Over Julius Erving (1976)

This is, unequivocally, the worst decision in franchise history. All of these other moves were trades that went wrong, but in the spirit of bad decisions, we’re going to cover this as well.

When the Nets were among the teams chosen to join the NBA after the ABA merger in 1976, the Knicks demanded that they pay a fee of $4.8 million (over 10 years) for encroaching on their territorial rights, a request that was sustained by the NBA alongside their $3.2 million fee for joining the league. In total, the Nets had to come up with $8 million just to exist.

The Knicks would get their money, alongside eventually suing the Nets and forcing them to move from Long Island to New Jersey, but made an unforgivable, disgusting error in the process.

Dr. J made $350,000 during this time, but wanted a renegotiation. As such, the Nets were willing to offload his salary and offered him to the Knicks, then owned by the Graham Paige Corporation and ran by Eddie Donovan in the front office.

The Knicks said no. They chose a few million, which was a lot at the time to be fair, over a future Hall of Famer.

Philadelphia purchased Erving for $3 million, and the rest is history. The Knicks let a rival get the best incoming ABA talent available and watched him lead the Sixers to a championship in 1983 while spending over a decade as a top-five player in the game.

Oh yeah, not to mention that the Knicks were mostly irrelevant during his time in the league and got swept twice by the Sixers in 1978 and 1983. Imagine if the Knicks could’ve gone from Clyde and Willis Reed to Dr. J. Ugh.

Maurice Lucas to the Suns (July 1982)

Truck Robinson Maurice Lucas

In the time between the Knicks’ eras of relevance in the 70s and 90s, it wasn’t anything too bad in the 80s, just inconsistency as they waited for the next big thing in Patrick Ewing to get them back into contention.

They seemed to stumble upon something huge in the summer of 1981, when the New Jersey Nets sent them a 28-year-old Maurice Lucas as a form of compensation for signing Ray Williams in free agency. Think of it as a precursor to a sign-and-trade. Nonetheless, the team got a former All-Star and All-Defense power forward still in his athletic prime.

In his one year in New York, Lucas averaged 15.8 points and 11.3 rebounds while shooting 50.3% from the field. It was his best overall season since he was in Portland, but the Knicks never saw him a long-term option, shipping him to Phoenix for Truck Robinson one year later.

The deal made sense at the time, as Robinson was even more productive than Lucas the season prior, but he hit hard regression in his age-31 season in 1982-83 and only lasted two seasons in New York, flaming out by age 33. He would hear it from the fans, being nicknamed “Dump Truck” for his startling fall-off.

Meanwhile, Lucas made his fifth All-Star team in his first year in Phoenix as part of a second prime that slowly dissipated a few years later. While Lucas would only have 2-3 years of All-Star level talent post-trade, it was a helluva lot better than Robinson.

They could’ve used that force at PF, you know. Bernard King and Bill Cartwright carried the Knicks to consecutive playoff appearances in 1983 and 1984, with the latter team being a game away from the Eastern Conference Finals. Just imagine how it would go if Lucas were there instead of Robinson.

Then again, if not for the dismantling of that team following the 1983-84 season, Ewing might not have ever been a Knick. Food for thought.

Rod Strickland To San Antonio (February 1990)

Maurice CheeksRod Strickland

The Knicks had their reasons for making this trade, it just aged badly.

Strickland was a solid backup point guard in his first year and a half in the league, but was blocked by Mark Jackson. The Knicks, who had risen to become a perennial playoff team in the late 80s, were thinking about getting to the next level, so they traded a young guard who was blocked for a 33-year-old veteran who could fit the role better as one of the league’s best defensive guards.

Cheeks, an NBA champion in Philly in 1983 and again as an assistant on this year’s staff, played a total of 107 games as a Knick, averaging eight points and five assists while adequately raising his game in the postseason. He was shipped out prior to 1991-92 for a pick that became Charlie Ward before retiring a year later. The player they got was fine, but they definitely could’ve used Strickland.

Jackson had a ceiling as a Knick, one that he reached quite early and led to his departure after 1991-92. Strickland, meanwhile, would become a great starting guard in San Antonio and Portland, eventually averaging 19 points and nine assists in his prime during the mid-to-late 90s.

I wonder if an offensively challenged Knicks team, one that relied on gritty defense without a true point guard and having to rely on John Starks (more of a 2-guard) to provide playmaking. Imagine if Strickland was the point guard instead of Doc Rivers in 1994.

The Eddy Curry Fiasco (October 2005)

Eddy Curry, Antonio DavisJermaine Jackson, Mike Sweetney, Tim Thomas, 2006 NYK 1st, 2007 Pick Swap, 2007 NYK 2nd, 2009 NYK 2nd

Isiah Thomas is damn lucky I’m only including one of his trades.

This was really bad. Eddy Curry was a fine player for the Bulls, one who was worth a decent salary and averaged 16 points and five rebounds at the end of his rookie contract. Putting aside the fact that he was seven-foot and grabbed way less rebounds than an average center, it’s a fine guy to trade for.

But that much? In a sign-and-trade? And you give him $60 million over six years to make the 23-year-old the sixth-highest-paid center in basketball? After seeing the Bulls drag their feet on an extension because of an irregular heartbeat? Seriously?

The players they gave up weren’t a big deal. Jermaine Jackson never played for the Bulls. Mike Sweetney replaced Curry as the starting center and was much worse before being out of the league by 2008. Tim Thomas played just three games as a Bull before being cut.

It’s the picks. It’s the hubris of believing the team was an Eddy Curry away from turning things around.

When Leon Rose traded a mountain of picks for Mikal Bridges, he understood that it might not result in a championship and assumed risk down the road, but also knew it wouldn’t immediately blow up due to the team having a very high floor as constructed. Worst-case scenario, the Nets get good picks in 2029 and 2031, not 2025 or 2027.

The Knicks won just 33 games the year before. They added Curry, Jerome James, Nate Robinson, and rookies Channing Frye and David Lee, and hired the man who won a title with a Pistons team that was better than the sum of its parts two years prior. They made a gamble that it would all work.

It didn’t. At all. They won just 23 games despite James Dolan paying luxury tax. They had the second-worst record in basketball, and they’d get nothing for it. The Bulls got the No. 2 pick in the draft and had future All-Star LaMarcus Aldridge fall into their lap. Now, they messed that up by sending him to Portland for Tyrus Thomas and Viktor Khryapa, but the point remains.

The following year, the Knicks won just 33 games after Isiah took over as head coach. The Bulls won a bunch more, exercising the swap and taking the No. 9 pick, which became future Defensive Player of the Year Joakim Noah.

The two top picks traded for Curry became two of the best big men of their generation. The second picks didn’t result in much, but the Bulls traded the 2007 2nd for Thabo Sefolosha and the 2009 2nd in a weird future swap with Portland, but the damage remains.

As for Curry on the Knicks, he had a great 2006-07, averaging 19.5 points and seven rebounds. After that, with four years left on his contract, he played a total of 69 more games as a Knick as he battled injuries, his weight, and a bad work ethic. Complete, franchise-altering disaster.

Tracy McGrady Becomes a Knick (February 2010)

Tracy McGrady, Sergio RodriguezJordan Hill, Jared Jeffries, Hilton Armstrong, Kevin Martin, 2011 Pick Swap, 2012 NYK 1st Joey Dorsey, Carl Landry, Larry Hughes

This trade wasn’t catastrophic by any means, but it’s inclusion is meant to represent all the times over the years that management traded draft picks for absolutely no reason, headlined by its most baffling.

A first-round pick, a swap, the guy you picked in the lottery literally eight months ago, and Jared Jeffries… for a 31-year-old rental who’s past his prime. It embodies the incompetence of the Knicks back then.

Jordan Hill wasn’t good, but they picked him between Steph Curry and DeMar DeRozan in June 2009. It’s ridiculous to give up on this guy that quickly, and it says a lot about the front office’s drafting ability and thought process. Jeffries and Hughes were okay role players. None of these guys would come back to bite you.

But like the Curry trade, it’s the damn picks. The 2011 swap didn’t convey because, unlike Isiah, Donnie Walsh actually added good players in between to ensure no collapse, as Amar’e Stoudemire lifted the Knicks to the postseason in 2011 (disregard that Houston had a better record and the West being a gauntlet was the only reason the swap didn’t convey). The 2012 pick landed at No. 16, but the 2012 draft was hilariously shallow, so Royce White doesn’t come back to bite him.

As for McGrady and Rodriguez? Neither of them played for the Knicks past April 2010. McGrady, particularly, played abysmally in 24 starts down the stretch and had to settle for a veteran minimum with the Pistons that summer. For a team that, at the time of the trade, was well below .500, it’s completely inconceivable.

Well, I guess it was meant to open up cap space for LeBron and company that offseason, and while Amar’e was a solid consolation prize (for a minute), the franchise’s incompetence at that point made it rather foolish to think the best player in the world was dying to come there. Good thing we didn’t do this again nine years later!

Acquiring Carmelo Anthony (February 2011)

Carmelo Anthony, Renaldo Balkman, Chauncey Billups, Anthony Carter, Shelden Williams, Corey BrewerWilson Chandler, Raymond Felton, Danilo Gallinari, Timofey Mozgov, Kosta Koufos, 2014 NYK 1st, 2016 Pick Swap, 2012 GSW 2nd, 2013 NYK 2ndEddy Curry, Anthony Randolph, 2015 DEN 2nd

Here’s a bold one, and no, I’m not saying this as someone who doesn’t like Melo. He was my favorite Knick when I first got into this team and I’ll always have a soft spot for him. The trade itself is relatively fine; the problem lies with the circumstances surrounding it.

Melo was due to be an unrestricted free agent that summer. The Knicks had plenty of space to give him the new max contract he desired from Denver. Instead of waiting until the summer to pair him with Amar’e in a move many believed was obvious, a paranoid Donnie Walsh was terrified of the crosstown Nets getting him instead, with the whole “Jay-Z as part-owner” schtick. Melo was not choosing the damn Nets, but the Knicks weren’t taking that risk.

It was a huge, 13-player trade, one that also involved dumping Curry’s contract to Minnesota. Let’s break down the guys that came with Melo, who’s story in New York is well known already:

  • Renaldo Balkman, who was drafted by the Knicks and traded to Denver in July 2008, played just 17 games after this trade in the next two seasons.
  • 34-year-old Chauncey Billups actually played very well in 21 starts down the stretch as an expiring contract, which convinced the Clippers he still had it (he played just 42 games in the next two seasons).
  • Anthony Carter played 19 games as a Knick before signing with the Raptors that offseason. He played his last game in 2011-12.
  • Shelden Williams played 17 games (started six) down the stretch. The big man ended his career with New Jersey the following season, playing just 58 more games.
  • Corey Brewer spent six days on the roster before being waived. He won a ring in Dallas that year, and his best years were ahead of him. Whoops.

As for what they gave up? Felton would eventually return a few years later, but the other three had solid NBA careers where they made a lot of money (looking at you, Mozgov). Gallinari’s marksmanship and Chandler’s solid play as a bench wing could’ve been useful off the bench during the Knickstape era, but they were just so horrified of Jay-Z.

The real kicker is the picks, again. Not that they were too damaging, just how funny it wound up being:

  • 2012 GSW 2nd: Landed No. 38, turned into Quincy Miller. Unrelated, Khris Middleton went one pick later. Good job, Nuggies.
  • 2013 GSW 2nd: Landed No. 51 and was traded to Orlando in the complicated Dwight Howard trade. Became Romero Osby, who never played in the NBA. Did I mention they got these two seconds for trading away David Lee?
  • 2014 NYK 1st: Landed No. 12 after a shockingly bad 2013-14 season, but was also sent to Orlando in Dwight trade. Became Dario Saric, who was then sent to Philly

Then there’s the 2016 pick swap. Both Denver and New York stunk in 2015-16, but the Knicks did lose one more game, landing them the No. 7 pick, which would then go to Denver. That became All-Star guard Jamal Murray.

I got good news and bad news from here.

Good news: by virtue of the swap, the Knicks landed the No. 9 pick in the draft, so the swap wasn’t that bad!

Bad news: because of the next trade, they didn’t make that selection.

The Andrea Bargnani Trade (July 2013)

Andrea BargnaniMarcus Camby, Steve Novak, Quentin Richardson, 2016 Swap Worst w/DEN, 2014 OKC 2nd, 2017 NYK 2nd

Vibes were high in the Summer of ‘13. After all, the Knicks had gotten to the second round of the playoffs for the first time in 13 years. Sure, it was a disappointing exit at the hands of the Pacers, but they felt as if their core still had some mileage in it with Melo, Amar’e, Tyson Chandler, Mike Woodson, and friends.

Let’s add another chef to the mix. Enter Bargnani, a failure of a No. 1 pick who enjoyed some solid seasons as Chris Bosh’s second fiddle before becoming a 20-PPG scorer in 2010-11. The two seasons before the trade, he was limited to 65 games, while his stretch-four abilities waned and his three-point shooting regressed sharply. An elbow injury suffered the year before the trade seemed not to dissuade management.

The players they gave up were more sentimental than skilled. Camby was a remnant of the transition from Ewing to Houston/Sprewell, having rejoined the Knicks that past season for the final 24 games of his career at age-38. Richardson was effectively the same, having played one game in 2012-13 in his second stint as a Knick after a nice, four-year run in the 2000s before retiring. Discount Double Check was a fan-favorite sniper, but one that was moved on from at the right time as his minutes and production completely cratered post-trade.

Once again, it’s the picks.

The OKC 2nd landed at No. 59 and was worthless. The 2017 pick landed at No. 36, which was eventually sent to Philly and became Jordan Bolden. Good thing this wasn’t a 2018 pick, phew. The real problem was a swap

The Knicks elected to make a rare move, trading the back end of a pick swap they had already traded. Essentially, Toronto got the worst of their picks and Denver’s picks. The odds of that being in the lottery were slim, but it handed Jakob Poeltl, a solid NBA big man for the last decade, right to them at No. 9.

As for Bargnani’s Knicks career, he sucked. He was the poster child of the team’s failure to maximize the rest of Melo’s prime, as Amar’e regressed hard, Chandler was traded, and this guy made eight figures to make boneheaded decision after boneheaded decision while battling injury. He played just 71 games as a Knick, made $23 million, and was dumped out the door after 2014-15. What a waste.

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Al Orth
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
There are several forgotten heroes from Yankees’ baseball prior to when the franchise started to win championships. Not that they didn’t have good years as a team in that time, but the pre-Babe Ruth years tend to blend together in a lot of fans’ minds.

One of those forgotten heroes was Al Orth, whose 1906 could be in the discussion for best seasons by a Yankee pitcher.

September 5, 1872 (Sedalia, MO) October 8, 1948 (Lynchburg, VA) 1904-09

While he was born in Missouri, Al Orth lived much of his early life in Indiana. There’s not a ton out there about his early life other than that he eventually attended DePauw University in Greencastle, IN. At some point, he developed an ability for baseball and begins showing up in on minor league rosters at 22-years-old, playing for the Lynchburg Hill Climbers in 1895.

In Lynchburg, Orth very quickly began to catch the eye of major league teams. After 269 good innings in 1895, Lynchburg sold him to the Phillies later that season. He went on to debut and throw 88 more innings in Philly that year, and put up a very solid, for that year, 3.89 ERA.

Over the next several years, while he had his ups and down, Orth became a fixture on the Phillies’ roster, and a mostly solid one at that. Known as the “Curveless Wonder,” Orth got his success from just varying the speed of his pitches as opposed to getting great movement. With the exceptions of 1895-96 — when he was still breaking into the bigs — and 1899, Orth threw at least 250 innings every season in Philadelphia and also posted at least 14 wins in all except his debut 1895. However, the Phillies never really got all that close to a NL pennant in his time there.

Orth had his best year as a Phillie in 1901. That year, he went 20-12 with a 2.27 ERA (151 ERA+), and recorded a league high six complete game shutouts. However, something else also happened in 1901: the American League was founded. Many NL mainstays started making the jump over, and Orth did so too, joining the Washington Senators for a reported $3500.

Despite moving to the still developing league from the “Senior Circuit,” Orth struggled in Washington. In 84 appearances over three seasons with the Senators, ho posted a 4.21 ERA, which equated to a 79 ERA+, as baseball began to enter the “deadball era.” He dropped off even further in 1904, leading to a July trade that sent him to the New York Highlanders.

The move to the Highlanders led to a rejuvenation for Orth. He was much better over the rest of 1904 — helping New York nearly swipe the AL pennant — and was again solid in 1905. Then in 1906, he put together his best career season. In New York, Orth joined a pitching staff that featured “spitballer” Jack Chesbro. With help from Chesbro, Orth began to throw the spitball himself, leading to a standout 1906. In a league-leading 338.2 innings, Orth put up a 2.34 ERA (127 ERA+), with 27 wins. According to modern stats, Orth was worth 8.1 rWAR and 6.0 fWAR, putting him among the league’s best that season.

Orth was okay the next year, but the Highlanders fell way back in the standings, and Orth ended up leading the league in losses. It was the first time ever a pitcher went from having the most wins to the most losses in consecutive years. After an even worse year in 1908, Orth seemingly left the majors, moved to Virginia and was set to be a player-manager in the Virginia League.

However, new Highlanders’ manager George Stallings lured Orth back for 1909. He only threw three innings on the mound and instead filled a new role. Orth had always been a pretty solid hitter, and not even for just pitcher standards, with a career 92 OPS+. Stallings used Orth as a pinch-hitter and in a handful of games at second base, and he put up a 113 OPS+ for the year.

Following that season, Orth did leave the majors and played for a couple minor league teams, including back in his new home in Lynchburg. He then returned to the majors in 1912, albeit as an umpire. He was the home plate ump for a 1912 game where pitchers Hippo Vaughn and Fred Toney both had no-hitters through nine innings. Toney completed his in 10 innings, after his Reds’ teammates scored a run on two hits in the top of the 10th.

Orth was a NL ump through 1917, at which point he left that role. Back in Virginia, he had stints as the baseball coaches at Washington & Lee University and the Virginia Military Institute. He resided in the area until his death in 1948 at age 76.

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

items.title: Gasly and Alpine stun Mercedes to take Italian GP pole
items.author: Ben Anderson
items.content:
Pierre Gasly claimed a shock pole position for the Alpine Formula 1 team in Italian Grand Prix qualifying at Monza, beating George Russell's Mercedes to the top spot.

The recently upgraded Alpine looked top-10 fast through practice but no one was expecting it to be a pole threat come qualifying.

Yet Gasly was super quick from the earliest runs in Q1, where he was fastest of all and team-mate Franco Colapinto was fourth.

Q2 was slightly tougher, where Gasly ended up fourth behind Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes and the two McLarens of Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris, while Colapinto slipped to eighth.

But in the top-10 shootout Gasly came back into the picture, lapping just 0.071s behind Russell's Mercedes on the first Q3 runs, and placing third behind Piastri's McLaren.

And on the final runs, even though Russell found 0.083s thanks to a tow from Max Verstappen, Gasly found more by following a Ferrari to claim his first pole position in F1 by 0.06s.

Piastri locked up at the first chicane on his final Q3 run, but his first lap was still good enough for third - though questions remain as to whether he may be penalised for impeding Liam Lawson's Red Bull in Q2.

The Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were fourth and fifth, after narrowly avoiding Q2 elimination, where Gabriel Bortoleto's Audi almost eliminated Hamilton and was only 0.008s slower than Leclerc.

Verstappen's Red Bull rounded out the top six, ahead of championship leader Antonelli, who sacrificed his Q3 to aid Russell's pole bid.

Antonelli will drop to the back of the grid thanks to taking a new engine for this weekend.

Colapinto was eighth in the second Alpine, ahead of Norris, whose final Q3 lap was compromised by Piastri's Turn 1 lock-up - robbing Norris of a lap-long tow.

Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10 for Racing Bulls, just 0.03s down on the 2025 world champion.

Bortoleto missed out on Q3, just 0.001s down on Hamilton's Ferrari, ruing a slide in the middle of the Ascari chicane, but he will anyway start 10th thanks to Antonelli's grid penalty.

Ollie Bearman's Haas, Nico Hulkenberg's Audi, the compromised Red Bull of Lawson, the Williams of Carlos Sainz and Esteban Ocon's Haas were the other cars eliminated in Q2.

In Q1 it was Yuki Tsunoda's Racing Bulls and Alex Albon's Williams that joined the expected Cadillacs and Aston Martin-Hondas in being eliminated.

Tsunoda was told to calm down on team radio after the session, while Albon was thanked by Williams for helping tow Sainz into Q2.

Valtteri Bottas was only 0.008s slower than Albon's Williams in the battle at the back, where Fernando Alonso's Aston Martin, which didn't make a second run in Q1, was more than half a second slower than Sergio Perez's Cadillac as energy-starved Monza brutally exposed the upgraded Honda engine's remaining power shortfall.

items.title: BTCC Croft: Cook dominates qualifying race
Finistere Ladies Classic: Sarah Van Dam takes the win after a photo finish
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Sarah Van Dam (Visma-Lease a Bike) surged from a six-rider breakaway to edge Lily Williams (Human Powered Health) in a photo–finish victory at the Finistère Ladies Classic.

Eva Van Agt (FDJ United-SUEZ) grabbed the final spot on the podium ahead of Maeva Squiban (UAE Team L'IMAD) and Kiara Lylyk (Mayenne-Mobana-Mypie), while Amber Kraak (Visma-Lease a Bike) was two seconds back for sixth.

With 40km to go, Van Agt, Van Dam and Squiban were the first movers for a decisive break and soon joined by Williams and Lylyk.

Originally a group of five which Kraak joined in the closing kilometres, the final sprint was instigated by Williams on the far left side of the finish straight. Lylyk tried to move past on the right side, but Van Dam blasted through the middle and was the only rider to hold off Williams.

"This victory means a lot to me. I’ve come close to winning my first race several times, and today everything fell into place," Van Dam said in a team statement about her first pro victory.

"Last week, I made a mistake in the sprint at the Kreiz Breizh Elites Féminin and finished third. I’ve learned from all those close finishes, and today I was finally rewarded with a victory."

The Saturday UCI 1.1 opener for a weekend of races on the Cap Sizun peninsula in France, Finistère Ladies Classic began in Pouldreuzic. The northbound course along the Brittany coastline crossed the finish line in Plouhinic just 18km into the start, which then presented eight laps of a hilly 9.5km circuit.

Each clockwise lap included an uncategorised 1.5km climb of 4.1% average gradient, leaving 3.5km the finish line, with the final approach uphill as well. Six times on the circuit provided intermediate sprint points in Plouhinec.

Rosita Reijnhout (Visma-Lease a Bike), Solene Muller (St Michel-Preference Home-Auber93) and Ema Comte (Cofidis) pulled away from the peloton on the opening laps. Once they were pulled back, another attack proved more successful by five other riders.

Once at the mid-point of the finish laps, Eva Van Agt (FDJ United-SUEZ), Maeva Squiban (UAE Team L'IMAD), Lily Williams (Human Powered Health), Sarah Van Dam (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Kiara Lylyk (Mayenne-Bonbana-MyPie) had a 30-second gap .

Once through the start-finish with three laps to go, a solo chase by Nikola Noskova (Cofidis) had her 30 seconds away from the breakaway group. The peloton trailed another 42 seconds back, with EF Education-Oatly taking over with the pacemaking.

The quintet stamped out a steady tempo and never saw Noskova get closer, as with two laps to go the peloton closed down her effort. The peloton hovered at a minute in arrears over the next 15km, no attacks launched from the group.

The breakaway group surged across the uphill road into Plouhinec for a ninth time all together, and in the closing kilometres Kraak joined the group after a long chase. The six riders would sprint for the victory, with the photo-finish going to Canadian Van Dam by the slightest of margins.

items.title: Tour of Britain Men: Cees Bol scores decisive sprint win on stage 4 while breakaway partner Tim Wellens takes GC lead
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Cees Bol won the gritty fourth stage of the Tour of Britain Men on Saturday, the Decathlon-CMA CGM rider surviving from the day’s break going ahead of Tim Wellens (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) in the Yorkshire Dales town of Leyburn.

Former Belgian champion Wellens started the day in second place overall, 12 seconds behind race leader Lewis Askey (NSN), his teammates working hard to set up an attack. That move came over 40km from the line, Wellens attacking from a peloton reduced to just a handful of riders on the day’s final classified climb at Redmire.

Reaching the breakaway close to the top of the tough climb, Wellens collected Bol, the pair building their lead on the plateau and the ensuing descent.

It was far from straightforward for the leading duo though, and the chasing group was within 30 seconds with one kilometre to go. Fabio Christen (Pinarello-Q36.5) broke clear from that chase group to finish third, 21 second behind Bol.

Despite having two teammates and help from other teams for the final run into the finish in the North Yorkshire town of Leyburn, Askey, who won the race’s opening stage on Wednesday meanwhile, finished fifth, 27 seconds behind Wellens.

That place means Askey drops to second drops to second place overall, 21 seconds behind Wellens, with one stage to go.

It’s unexpected for me," said Bol whose other career victories have come in bunch sprints. "I was going the going in the break actually to help my teammate Daan [Hoole], but I found myself in the leading group on the on the top of the last climb, and then I knew the stage win was possible."

"I mean, he was he was going to win the GC, so he did most of the work, he was really strong," Bol said of Wellens. "Hats off to him for taking the leader’s jersey. I gave him some pulls, and normally on the sprint I'm faster, and we both knew that, I think, so that's why the cooperation was good.

"I was suffering really hard because there was still a small hill, 2km to go, and Tim was really keeping the pace high there, so just suffering and focusing to to not let the wheel go, and then from the top there I didn't pull anymore, and then I knew I could could win."

The queen stage of this year’s Tour of Britain saw the peloton remain in Yorkshire, racing 165.8km from Helmsley to Leyburn in the Yorkshire Dales. Climbing 2,169 metres, the route contained three classified climbs, two first-category and one second, and with the final two kilometres almost all uphill, with short gradients into double figures, a bunch sprint was not guaranteed.

It was an aggressive start to the day, with riders from the five WorldTour teams in the race particularly active in trying to form a breakaway. Finally, with almost 20km done, six riders escaped, former British champion Ben Swift (Netcompany-Ineos) with Cees Bol (Decathlon-CMA CGM), Xandro Meurisse (Pinarello-Q36.5), Ian López (Modern Adventure), Brem Deman (Flanders-Baloise) and Boas Lysgaard (BHS-PL Baton Bornholm) quickly building a lead over the bunch approaching two minutes.

With the gap out to five minutes on the climb of Greenhow, the UAE Team Emirates-XRG team of Tim Wellens, who started the day in second place overall, upped the pace, hoping to trouble race leader Lewis Askey (NSN).

Despite their efforts, Askey survived, though behind him the peloton split and the breakaway’s advantage reduced to 3:13 as they crested the climb, with 96km remaining. While the peloton re-formed, UAE stayed on the front, gradually reducing the peloton’s deficit to 1:10 as the base of the day’s final classified climb at Redmire was reached.

With an average gradient of 8.1% over its 3.5 kilometres, the climb was sure to take its toll and not only did the peloton explode, but Askey began to slip backwards, UAE still applying pressure. With Askey drifting further back, Wellens made his move, the former Belgian champion reaching solo leader Meurisse just before the top of the climb.

Over the top Wellens was with Bol, the two riders almost 50 seconds ahead of Askey’s group, as they took on the long descent into Wensleydale before the final run to the line. Despite having two teammates to support him through the final 40k, Askey’s deficit slipped to a maximum of 1:20, even though Bol initially refused to lend the Belgian a hand.

Askey, on the other hand, had help, riders from Netcompnay-Ineos, Tudor Pro Cycling and Pinarello-Q36.5 all riding on the front and bringing the deficit to within one minute with 19km left.

Though the gap remained around the minute mark with 10km to go Wellens was rocking and rolling on his bike, the effort beginning to show, however, he and Bol managed to stay ahead to fight for the stage win.

items.title: Yankees Rivalry Roundup: Rays, Red Sox both gain ground; Guardians sweep doubleheader
items.author: Andrew Mearns
items.content:
The Yankees lost a tough one on Friday night, as they failed to score more than a Ben Rice solo shot against old nemesis Walker Buehler, and while Max Fried, Will Warren, and David Bednar admirably went toe-to-toe with a fierce Padres bullpen, it wasn’t enough. A 2-1 lead in the 10th vanished on one mighty swing of the bat by Luis Campusano against Paul Blackburn, who entered play with a 1.62 ERA. No shade at the pitching in this one, the offense just had to do more early on with Buehler. He’s better than he was in his nightmare 2025 with Boston, but not much better.

Here’s what else was afoot around the Junior Circuit on Friday. The loss was costly.

Tampa Bay Rays (84-57) 7, Texas Rangers (70-72) 6

Texas helped New York gain a half-game on the Thursday offday by blanking Tampa Bay 6-0, but six runs weren’t enough for the Rangers to be of any use on Friday. The Rays jumped back to four games ahead of the Yankees, doing most of their damage against former top prospect Kumar Rocker in a bulk relief appearance. Ezequiel Duran briefly gave Texas a 1-0 lead in the second, only for Tampa Bay to counter with six unanswered runs between the third and the fifth. Jonathan Aranda and Richie Palacios both hit solo shots, and in the fifth, Aranda sandwiched a double between two-baggers from Yandy Díaz and Junior Caminero.

Victor Mesa Jr. also had an RBI knock in the fifth as Tampa Bay’s lead grew to 6-1.

Give credit to the Rangers’ No. 9 hitter, catcher Elias Díaz. He is the primary reason why the Rays had to sweat this one out late. In the seventh, Texas drove Nick Martinez from the game with a one-out walk from Jake Burger and an Evan Carter single. Garrett Cleavinger entered, walked Cody Freeman to load the bases, and then coughed up a game-changing grand slam to Díaz.

As it turned out, the Rays needed the insurance run they got with one down in the ninth. Yandy singled off Trade Deadline acquisition Chase Silseth, Jorge Mateo pinch-ran and stole second, and after Aranda got plunked, Caminero drove in Mateo with a hit to center. Adam Macko then entered and stranded the runners, making it a 7-5 ballgame to begin the bottom of the ninth.

The Rangers had life in the ninth when Bryan Baker issued back-to-back walks to the first two batters; he was forced from the game rather quickly due to illness with his velocity down, too. Tyler Wells had to get the last three outs, and he pulled it off. Pinch-hitter Nicky Lopez bunted the runners into scoring position, Díaz played his fifth run with a sacrifice fly, and Justin Foscue popped up a 2-1 pitch to end it.

Boston Red Sox (77-65) 1, Baltimore Orioles (69-73) 0: I don’t know how many of you caught the Chris Sale shutout against the Dodgers a little over a week ago, but it played out in a somewhat-similar manner to this Red Sox/O’s game last night. Drake Baldwin led off that one with a homer off Yoshinobu Yamamoto for the first and only run of the night. Yamamoto was otherwise brilliant but LA never dented home plate against Sale and it was a 1-0 final.

Well, Ranger Suarez didn’t go as deep as Sale and Mickey Gasper homered on the second at-bat of the game rather than the first, but otherwise … pretty close! (Although I suppose Braves/Dodgers didn’t have the same benches-clearing feistiness.) Boston won its second straight one-run game at Camden Yards, with Suarez firing seven shutout frames before Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman slammed the door. The O’s only three at-bats all night with a runner in scoring position, and none resulted in hits. Shane Baz and the Baltimore bullpen did a very nice job, but no cigar. They’re in serious trouble now, losing a game and a half to Cleveland in the Wild Card race in one day, falling to three back. Meanwhile, Boston is 3.5 behind New York for the top Wild Card spot.

Chicago White Sox (74-67) 4, Minnesota Twins (67-74) 1: Chicago’s AL Central lead would be trimmed by half a game due to circumstances beyond their control, but the Pale Hose won their own game against the Twins. Miguel Vargas, Braden Montgomery, and Colson Montgomery all flexed their muscles with blasts off Zebby Matthews, and the White Sox threw shutout ball until the ninth. Vargas and Colson each registered their 30th homers of the season. Incidentally, we have not been tracking the Twins for a moment, but at 4.5 games behind Cleveland for the Wild Card with three teams ahead of them, they are all but toast.

Cleveland Guardians (71-70) 7, Detroit Tigers (64-76) 6 [Game 1] The perhaps-no-longer-Gritty Tigs’ season is utterly lost at this point, so they have to settle for trying to play spoiler for the team that rallied from a record 15.5 games down to swipe the AL Central from them in 2025. And they took a 6-2 lead in Cleveland by beating up on Logan Allen with two-run knocks from Ben Malgeri and Max Clark, as well as a solo shot by Spencer Torkelson. However, the doubleheader matinee turned into The Brayan Rocchio Show. He crushed a game-tying grand slam off Keider Montero in the fourth, and with it still knotted at 6-6 in the ninth, he launched the longest homer of his career to walk it off.

Cleveland Guardians (72-70) 4, Detroit Tigers (64-77) 3 [10 innings] [Game 2] The Guardos had so much fun walking the Tigers off in the opener that they decided to do it all over again in the nightcap. Once again, Detroit had the early advantage, tallying three off Trade Deadline acquisition Foster Griffin. The Guardians crawled back, and 2024 No. 1 pick Travis Bazzana swatted a two-run homer in the eighth to knot it up at 3-3. Bazzana must have taken notes from Rocchio because he got to tally the walk-off as well as that game-tying blast. Hunter Gaddis stranded the zombie runner in the top of the 10th with three groundouts, opening the door for Bazzana to end it on a single off Kenley Jansen with Rocchio on third following a pair of stolen bases. Cleveland’s twin bill sweep lifted their Wild Card lead to a game over Toronto.

Toronto Blue Jays (71-71) 9, Kansas City Royals (63-79) 2: Cleveland winning twice with the doubleheader always meant that the Jays would be losing ground of some kind to them in their late Wild Card chase. But they at least limited the damage to a half-game loss. Although old friend/two-time Tommy John surgery recipient Jameson Taillon had to leave with dreaded elbow discomfort, his offense picked him up. Everyone in the starting lineup outside of Charles McAdoo had at least one hit, with Ernie Clement, Alejandro Kirk, and George Springer all delivering RBI doubles.

Houston Astros (73-69) 3, Arizona Diamondbacks (74-68) 1: Not much to touch on from this one because neither of these teams are very interesting. Cristian Javier fired five frames of one-hit, one-run ball, fanning eight, and batterymate Yainer Diaz kicked off the scoring for Houston with a solo shot against Merrill Kelly. The ’Stros tacked on more in the third when Isaac Paredes doubled in Jeremy Peña, and Jose Altuve plated Yordan Alvarez on a sacrifice fly. The Rangers’ loss means that Houston has a fairly comfortable three-game lead, aided by an Astros edge in the head-to-head tiebreaker.

items.title: 'Sometimes he falls into that trap of wanting too much' – Decathlon admit potential weakness for Felix Gall in Vuelta a España red jersey battle
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
According to his Decathlon CMA CGM team, Felix Gall is only just approaching his favoured terrain at the Vuelta a España: the most vicious, long and steep climbs, and with a solid buffer to defend his spot on the podium, it could open the door to more adventurous attacking from the Austrian.

Having utilised his strong climbing core several times to put his rivals to the sword, Gall has been a step below Mas on the toughest days so far, but having put solid distance between his third place and Richard Carapaz and Oscar Onley, who sit 1:47 and 2:23 behind him in fourth and fifth overall, could now be the best time to throw caution to the wind?

"For sure," said Decathlon sports director Luke Roberts to when asked that very question ahead of stage 12. "It's too much to say the podium is secure, but we have a nice buffer to fourth place, so we can change our tactics a little bit, and look to target the guys ahead of us without having to worry too much about the guys behind us anymore. Put it that way."

Unfortunately for Roberts, Decathlon suffered a major hit as stage 13 got underway on Thursday, when Gregor Mühlberger – Gall's "best friend and good motivator," according to Roberts – crashed out of the race, leaving him without his top climbing domestique who had been sat in ninth overall.

This may throw a spanner into the works when it comes to changing up how they approach the racing, having previously just been operating with a very Team Sky-train to lead out Gall on the previous mountain days.

"The longer and steeper the climb is, the better it's going to suit Felix. And until now, we've had some steeper sections on climbs, but nothing that's been steep all the way to the line, basically," said Roberts.

"Some days like that are still to come. [Today] will be more suited to Felix, so, as I said, until now we've put the pressure on, done what we could on those days, and now we'll be ready to really target the ones that suit Felix."

Handling the mental pressure of Grand Tour GC racing

Roberts praised Gall for how he's been handling the mental pressure of taking on a second Grand Tour in 2026, especially this time racing with overall victory as a realistic outcome, but also admitted how, at times, his eagerness to perform can come back to bite him.

"I think he's handling it quite well. I did quite a bit of work with him before the Giro, just on how he approaches the racing, his attitude towards it. In the past, he's often had a reputation for being overambitious or trying too much," said Roberts.

"We tried to have him look at things a bit differently and have a calmer approach to the race and focus a bit more on what he do, rather than what he perhaps do. At the Giro, he managed it really well and gained a lot of confidence out of that.

"Sometimes he falls into that trap of pushing too much, wanting too much, but slowly he starts to be a bit more relaxed, and he sees his goal of the podium becoming more and more realistic here. He sees what he's capable of, and we're confident going into the second half of the race."

Unfortunately for Gall's chances of chasing red, they may simply have to concede that Mas is stronger, whatever the tactics employed, as was the case to Alto de Aitana last weekend and Calar Alto on Thursday, but even still, podiums at two Grand Tours in the same year would mean a stunning year for Gall, who has really found his best form in 2026.

"Once Pogačar unfortunately left the race, the race changed completely. But our goal is to aim for a podium place here – that doesn't change even with Pogačar leaving the race," said Roberts.

"Obviously, winning becomes more possible than just aiming for that podium place, and we want to keep the pressure on. Last Sunday [on stage 9], the timing was off, and the boys were maybe a bit overambitious.

"Then [on Calar Alto] we just tried to shake the tree a bit and see if one of the three closest contenders to us for the podium might drop, and it was Oscar Onley that did. But in the end, when Mas attacked, he's riding incredibly strong at the moment; there's not a lot we can do when he goes.

"We've still got quite a way to go in the race, and obviously still some climbs to come that are going to suit Felix a lot more. So it's up to us to keep putting the pressure on and see if we can secure that podium place and yeah, even try to step up a place or two."

items.title: The Yankees Reliever Confidence Index: September Edition
items.author: Nick Power
items.content:
As the Yankees enter the season’s final month, a bullpen that’s been a strength throughout the year is running on fumes. Injuries to Fernando Cruz and Kervin Castro have further strained an already thin unit, forcing the Yankees to get creative in adding some veteran talent from outside their organization for the stretch run.

As I do each month in a given season, I’m going to take a look at the Yankees’ relievers to identify how manager Aaron Boone is deploying each and offer a verdict as to how much trust we can place in them moving forward using the following ranking system:

  • : As confident as one can be in a reliever, the most fickle position in baseball
  • : High degree of confidence, but some trepidation remains
  • : Glass half full or glass half empty? The choice is yours
  • : Major concerns here, though perhaps a glimmer of hope
  • : Absolute zero — usually reserved for those with a minimal track record

Statistics below are from August 6-September 2.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP, Saves (in 7 opportunities)

After a couple of days off and with the rest of the bullpen gassed, Bednar came in to eat the eighth inning of what was then a 7-1 blowout at the hands of the Angels on Monday. He allowed three runs, inflating his stats in garbage time. The right-hander allowed only one other earned run all August, though, cementing his status as one of the game’s most reliable closers.

No one in baseball has finished more games than Bednar’s 50 this year, and he’s done it while blowing just three saves. He isn’t as flashy as some of the game’s other elite late-inning arms, but he’s been as effective as any of them.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP

It’s been a choppier month than we’ve seen before from Headrick this year. Opponents hit .345 with a 1.015 OPS against him in August, a red flag for a pitcher who’s made the second-most appearances in baseball. Still, even after his uneven stretch, the southpaw’s ERA sits below 2.00.

Headrick has shown enough to receive the benefit of the doubt here. Especially after the injury to Cruz, who was among MLB’s most-used relievers before his injury, fatigue is a legitimate concern. But in a tight AL East race, expect Boone to continue deploying his fireman in big spots.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP

It’s been a rapid ascent for Blackburn, who began the season as the last man out of the bullpen and is now one of Boone’s most trusted relievers. He hasn’t skipped a beat since moving into a high-leverage role, allowing no earned runs across his last 16 appearances dating back to late July.

Like other Yankees reclamation projects before him, Blackburn has been able to leverage his sinker into a skyrocketing ground ball rate. There’s no reason at this point to believe the tweaks he’s made are not sustainable.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP

A week and change ago, Fulmer was out of a job after the Angels cut him loose. Now, he’s the Yankees’ new shiny toy, with the Joel Sherman relaying that the team feels they saw things in his video that other teams missed. With a dearth of options, he’s been thrown right into the fire. The early results have not been encouraging.

Fulmer has only made four appearance for the Yankees, so it’s too soon to say how valuable he will be. Any return to form would be a remarkable comeback for the 33-year-old, who’s appeared only sporadically in MLB since 2023.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP

Formerly ol’ reliable in this column, Hill’s stock took a major hit after a disastrous run from mid-May through mid-July in which he allowed 18 runs in 18 innings. He’s been better since, deployed strategically in mostly in lower-leverage spots.

Hill is not a back-end reliever, and that should be OK. The crafty lefty still serves a useful role, particularly against lefty batters, who are hitting .205 with a .575 OPS against him this year.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP (with Kansas City and New York)

Another new kid on the block, Schreiber made his Yankees debut on Tuesday, pitching a clean ninth to close out a victory against the Angels. The 32-year-old brings with him a long track record of steady bullpen performance, including this season. Schreiber posted a 3.65 ERA and 117 ERA+ in 56 appearances with Kansas City before they placed him on waivers as they drifted out of contention.

Some of Schreiber’s underlying metrics — including a .254 BABIP and 36:22 K:BB ratio with Kansas City — are cause for concern. Still, considering the Yankees got him for nothing, he’s a quality pickup given the slim pickings at this point in the season.

: IP, ERA, SO, FIP

Yarbrough has been something of a shadow starter for most of the season, appearing once a week or so to pitch multiple innings in relief and then retreating to obscurity in the bullpen. A four-run blowup against the Red Sox last week jumped his season ERA nearly a half-run, underscoring the limits of his bag of tricks.

Come playoff time, Yarbrough should only be seeing action if a game is out of hand. He’s been a perfectly serviceable placeholder this year, helping eat innings in a bullpen that’s seen its high performers used frequently.

: IP, ERA, SO (including minor leagues)

Gil’s wilderness period is over. After a disastrous start to the year for the Yankees and nearly four months spent on the IL, the team decided to bring their former Rookie of the Year back in a relief role. He tossed 7.1 scoreless innings across five appearances in the minors, and he made his return to the big leagues last Monday, allowing one run in two innings of work.

Gil’s is such a bizarre case that it’s difficult to place any stock in him. While unquestionably talented, the 27-year-old has endured consecutive lost seasons. Until he can prove otherwise, his superlative 2024 campaign is the clear outlier. Time will tell if he can reinvent himself in his new role.

items.title: 'We're not ruling out anything' - EF Education-EasyPost confirm Richard Carapaz's ongoing fight for overall in Vuelta a España
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
As stage 14's mountainous race to Sierra de Pandera gets underway, Carapaz is currently in fourth place, 3:53 back, and with a 36-second advantage over his closest pursuer, Oscar Onley (Netcompany Ineos).

The defending champion from the last time the Vuelta visited what is known as the 'Angliru of the South’, due to it’s asphyxiatingly narrow, ultra-steep upper slopes, Carapaz was the only GC challenger to launch a long-distance attack on the previous high-mountain stage, to Calar Alto.

The Ecuadorian climber's typically non-conformist move, some 40 kilometres from the finish, failed to gain enough traction for him to go clear. But given it was from so far out, it also sparked questions as to his top priority in a race where he has finished both on the final podium back in 2020 as well as taking multiple stages and the KoM jersey in 2022.

"We're here for a good overall placing and you can see that from the way he's been racing, he hasn't moved at all until making that attack," EF Education-EasyPost sports director Juanma Garate told

"He went for it on the Velefique" - the second last climb of the Calar Alto stage - "but then Ivan Romeo did an amazing job working for Movistar and [race leader] Enric Mas.

"We thought maybe that Carapaz' attack could cause Ivan to crack and Mas would be isolated and nobody would work in the bunch, particularly as Decathlon" - by common consent the strongest mountains team in the Vuelta this year - "were more likely to go for it in Calar Alto.

"So we tried to shake the tree a bit to keep moving up overall and that's our main idea."

In the stages that come up, it is harder to say if Carapaz will continue to try to go from distance, Garate said, pointing to the lack of suitable terrain until stage 20. The distance between major climbs is too great, Garate argues, and then the climbs themselves at Calar Alto, steep at the bottom then easing out for many kilometres before the summit, did not help getting in breaks either.

Apart from victory on Sierra de la Pandera, Carapaz also has a good history on the two big mountain stages yet to come. Stage 19 to Peñas Blancas was where he won in 2022, too, whilst in Sierra Nevada in 2024, which also featured the dauntingly difficult Puerto de El Purche, Carapaz launched a long-distance move and picked up two minutes advantage overall. He finally finished fourth, a placing which reconfirmed - he said at the time - his renewed aptitude for Grand Tour GC racing.

This time round, Carapaz came into the Vuelta fresh from taking two Alpine stage wins of a possible three at the Tour as well as the mountains title - for a second time. In the Vuelta, therefore, he's under no pressure to produce results, barring the pressure he puts on himself.

"So we're going to keep going for the general classification. Obviously if there's a stage win, we're not going to turn it down, but that's the idea. But the great thing in general is that he's always up for trying. He's really brave."

Although Carapaz' attacks often look like spontaneous affairs, the move on Velefique had been planned beforehand, Garate said. "We'd talked about it a lot, in the preceding days and in the team car as well. Movistar hadn't looked so strong - although judging by what they did in the Calar Alto stage, they've turned things around a lot - and having the leader's jersey in their ranks is giving them a lot of extra motivation.

"On other occasions he just goes for it because I can't see what he's doing from the team car. But that move was planned."

In keeping with his star rider's trademark refusal to accept the status quo, in terms of the GC, Garate himself is not putting any kind of upper limit on Carapaz's ambitions and not just because of the rider himself.

"We're hitting 40 degrees in these stages, the peloton is suffering a heck of a lot as a result, I heard there was even a rider in the bunch who blacked out [on stage 12]. It's recommended to the general public the don't go out in this kind of weather, when it's so hot, and we're out there riding our bikes."

"It's a really unpredictable situation. Enric Mas is very strong and looks solid, his team is working really well. But the Vuelta's always been a race where you can't rule out anything at all.

"Right now, Enric's the favourite, but [Primoz] Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) can overtake him in the time trial. People forget that we've got two flat stages in western Andalucia coming up where the wind can play a really important factor, too. Basically, anything could still happen."

items.title: Russell fastest in final Italian GP practice
items.author: Jack Cozens
items.content:
Mercedes Formula 1 driver George Russell marked himself out as favourite for Italian Grand Prix pole position by setting the pace in final practice at Monza.

Russell and team-mate Kimi Antonelli spent part of the session practicing the tows that are likely to play a significant role in the fight for pole position in qualifying, though Russell looked fast with and without assistance.

His final effort - a 1m22.219s that was three tenths clear of Friday's FP2 benchmark - came without a tow from Antonelli (who has grid penalties this weekend) and was 0.226s faster than the next-best time, set by Lewis Hamilton.

Max Verstappen was third as Red Bull's single-lap pace appeared in a much better place than on Friday, though he and Ferrari driver Hamilton did have a minor on-track altercation at the end of FP3 that was noted by the stewards.

Hamilton jumped ahead of Verstappen entering the Alboreto (Parabolica) corner, with Verstappen subsequently giving Hamilton a thumbs-up as they crossed the start/finish line to indicate his lap had been compromised and then running deep into the first corner to ensure Hamilton could not take the apex.

Championship leader Antonelli was fourth ahead of Lando Norris, the winner of the past two races, in the best of the McLarens.

His team-mate Oscar Piastri set the fastest first sector of all on his final attempt and was still inside Russell's benchmark through sector two, but ended the lap more than half a second down and only eighth-fastest - a clear indication of the varying energy deployment patterns teams are working to this weekend.

Between them were Charles Leclerc in the second Ferrari and the Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad, who for a while at the end of the session held the fastest final sector courtesy of a huge tow from the Audi of Nico Hulkenberg.

That partly accounted for Lindblad's gap to the next-best midfield driver, Pierre Gasly, who finished the session ahead of team-mate Franco Colapinto as the Alpine duo rounded out the top 10.

Liam Lawson had a difficult start to Saturday in the second Red Bull, looping his RB22 as he got on the power - and the kerb - through the first chicane. He finished the session in 12th, the best part of a second off Russell and more than six tenths down on Verstappen.

At the back, Fernando Alonso improved late on to lead the Aston Martin-Cadillac quartet that once again looks cut adrift.

items.title: Friends establish a GoFundMe page for Ezra Caudell as Modern Adventure provide an injury update
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
The Modern Adventure Pro Cycling team of Ezra Caudell have provided a brief update on the US rider’s condition as he remained in the ICU at Jefferson Einstein Philadelphia hospital, and have given details of a crowdfunding campaign.

While Menten was lucky to escape the incident with little more than whiplash injuries, Caudell’s injuries were much worse, and he remains in hospital a week after the incident.

"At present, Ezra continues to be supported by medical professionals with the support of his family by his side," the Modern Adventure team statement read.

"Further updates on his condition will be communicated by the team, in accordance with the wishes of the Caudell family, in due course. Until then, we respectfully ask that they be allowed the privacy and space they need at this difficult time, and to respect that we will share information only when, and if, it is appropriate to do so."

The team confirmed they had reached out to Menten to offer support, adding: "[We] recognize the difficult circumstances we now share surrounding this incident. We will continue to navigate this situation together, along with Ezra’s family, teammates and friends, supporting one another as we do so."

The team also explained that a close friend of Caudell’s family has established a GoFundMe page to help with his recovery.

Lotto-Intermarché also issued a statement on their social media. "Milan Menten was involved in the crash at the Philadelphia Cycling Classic. He sustained a whiplash injury but, all things considered, is physically doing okay.

"Milan’s thoughts are first and foremost with Ezra Caudell. Milan is in close contact with Ezra’s team.

"Lotto-Intermarché joins Milan in expressing its full support to Ezra, his family, teammates and those close to him."

The incident comes at a time when there is a huge focus on safety in races, especially after the recent death of Finlay Tarling at the Vuelta a Portugal.

The GoFundMe page was established on September 3 and in two days had raised $57,151 raised of a goal for $100,000 to support Caudell and his family. The page can be found .

items.title: Tadej Pogačar Won’t Race Again in 2026 and Montréal Worlds Is Suddenly Wide Open
items.author: ahood
items.content: The world No. 1 will miss Montréal worlds, the Europeans and Lombardia after his Vuelta crash and surgery. UAE not putting date on return.

items.title: Tadej Pogačar to miss remainder of 2026 season after Vuelta a España crash, but extends UAE Team Emirates-XRG contract until 2032
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
This means he will miss out on defending his titles at the World Championships in Canada, the European Championships at home in Slovenia, and Il Lombardia.

"Of course, this isn’t the way I wanted my season to finish. Right now, the most important thing is to recover properly and give my body the time it needs," said Pogačar.

"It has been a season with many special moments and I’m proud of what we achieved together. Now I’ll focus on getting healthy, supporting the guys from home, and coming back next year ready for what’s ahead."

"After consultation with the team’s medical and performance staff, the decision has been taken to prioritise his recovery and rehabilitation, allowing him the necessary time to return to full health without placing a timeline on his return to competition," read an announcement on the team's website.

Pogačar crashed out while leading the Vuelta on stage 8, as he looked to complete the set of Grand Tour overall titles, suffering a complex fracture to his collarbone, a stable C7 cervical fracture, cuts to his face, and a concussion.

After being transported to Barcelona by ambulance, he underwent surgery on Monday, August 31, before returning to his home in Monaco two days later. Pictures posted on social media by his partner, Urška Žigart, showed him leaving the hospital with his left arm in a sling, and with several bandages on his face and left knee.

"Tadej is progressing well following surgery and we are very satisfied with his recovery to this point. However, given the combination of his injuries – the concussion, the stable C7 cervical fracture and the open clavicle fracture – we have taken the decision, together with Tadej, that he will not return to competition this season," said team Medical Director, Dr. Adrian Rotunno.

"From a medical perspective, his health is paramount, and the priority now is to allow each of these injuries to heal fully and to progress through his rehabilitation in a controlled manner.

"The post-operative clavicle and cervical fracture will both require a structured period of rehabilitation. Equally important is the need for him to progress carefully through a graduated concussion recovery protocol, with ongoing neurological monitoring. Only once he is medically recovered and personally ready, clearance to gradually start increasing training load can be given.

"There is no benefit in accelerating that process simply to meet a racing deadline. Removing the pressure allows Tadej to focus entirely on his recovery, with the objective of returning to full training and competition when he is completely ready."

Pogačar's original plan was to complete the Vuelta on September 13, with two weeks to prepare for Worlds on September 27 – where he was chasing a third road race rainbow jersey in a row – but this, the Europeans on October 4, and a chance at a record sixth Lombardy crown on October 20 have all come too soon.

While he won't be seen at a race until 2027, UAE confirmed in the same announcement that he had extended his stay on the Emirati super team until 2032, putting to bed any suggestions of an early retirement after the LA Olympics in 2028 or in 2030, when his last contract was due to expire.

"Tadej has been central to the journey and development of this team, and we are extremely proud that this relationship will continue through 2032," said team principal and CEO Mauro Gianetti.

"Following his crash, there is absolutely no pressure for Tadej to return to racing this year. His health and recovery are the priority. He has given an enormous amount throughout the season and now the right decision is for him to take the necessary time to recover fully. We look forward to having him back with us when he is ready."

Pogačar's absence at the remaining key races of the season will completely change how they play out, but his extended time in the peloton points to a continuation of his domination, as the best rider seen since Eddy Merckx.

items.title: F2 reveals revised car to reflect F1 2026 changes
items.author: Josh Suttill
items.content:
Formula 2 has revealed a heavily modified car for the coming seasons at the Italian Grand Prix, bringing it closer to the look of Formula 1's current machine.

The revised car, which will retain the existing chassis, was revealed in the F1 paddock at Monza on Saturday and will be used in F1's primary feeder series from 2027 to 2029.

F2 last introduced a new car in 2024 to more closely mirror the look of F1's ground-effect-era cars used from 2022-25.

This new 2027 car better reflects the visual direction of F1's new 2026 cars but without being a complete overhaul, keeping costs lower.

Its aero package is also designed to allow cars to follow each other more closely.

The new car will be powered by the same 3.4-litre turbocharged V6 Mecachrome engine used in the 2024-26 generation.

And it will run on 18-inch wheelrims once more, having pioneered them on its 2020 car, two years before F1 adopted them.

The car will run on sustainable fuel, supplied by Aramco, partner of Aston Martin's F1 team.

For the first time, the car will feature an on-board starter, meaning stalled cars are less likely to be stranded.

F2 said this had been accomplished through the development of "an evolution of the current gearbox" from supplier Hewland.

It should be the car used by Lando Norris's brand-new LN4 Fusion team next year, led by former Prema leader Rene Rosin.

The team is yet to be officially granted an entry, but this is believed to be a formality.

items.title: Briatore-FIA row continues with appeal court response
items.author: Jack Cozens
items.content:
The FIA International Court of Appeal has issued a statement defending its processes in the wake of Alpine Formula 1 executive advisor Flavio Briatore's comments that appeared to question the independence of one judge on its panel.

Briatore started a public row against McLaren during a press conference appearance at the Italian Grand Prix on Friday. That came after the FIA communicated that its International Court of Appeal had ruled to reinstate the two five-second penalties that Pierre Gasly incurred at the Monaco GP in June, which Alpine had previously successfully had quashed.

This meant Gasly lost his podium for a second time, having crossed the line in third.

While Briatore said he accepted the decision, he also appeared to question the impartiality of one of the four ICA judges - Filippo Marchino - on the panel during the August hearing.

Reading from a piece of paper that he continued to refer to, Briatore claimed Marchino had been "very nasty during the hearing" and was "acting as a prosecutor".

"And after, we found out what is the reason why he's so nasty, this guy? He's very linked with McLaren. I'm very surprised this guy has the link with McLaren," Briatore said.

That McLaren mention is pertinent because it was one of two teams, alongside Red Bull, that had appealed the decision to reinstate Gasly to third place.

In a statement released on Saturday morning, the FIA Court of Appeal rejected any suggestion that the process of its selection of judges had not been impartial.

It did not name Briatore directly but said the comments related to case ICA-2026-06-07-08-09 - the hearing for the case brought by McLaren and Red Bull.

"The FIA courts wish to make clear that the appointment and participation of the judges in that case, like for any other case, were conducted in accordance with the applicable FIA judicial procedures and usual practice, which are inspired by the highest standards like the IBA guidelines on conflicts of interest in international arbitration," the FIA statement read.

"All judges are elected by the FIA general assemblies, some of them upon proposition of a group of at least five F1 teams in accordance with the FIA statutes.

"They are all subject to the independence and confidentiality requirements contained in the FIA judicial and disciplinary rules, make annual disclosures of interests to the FIA compliance officer, and sign a specific declaration of independence for each particular case in consideration of the issue at stake and the parties involved, which is served to the parties."

The International Court of Appeal has a roster of 36 leading legal experts, at least eight of whom are selected to be part of a pool that can be picked for each case.

This pool is communicated to relevant parties ahead of time to assess whether there are any "serious and objective reasons to consider that any or all of the shortlisted judges should be recused due to the existence of a conflict of interest or other legitimate grounds".

The statement said this had happened, with the relevant parties "invited to raise any issue concerning the proceedings or the composition of the court".

"None did so," the statement added. "No objection was raised during the hearing concerning the manner in which the court questioned the witness or conducted the proceedings.

"The ICA emphasises the importance of constituting panels with judges from different cultural and geographical backgrounds. This helps ensure that the deliberations and discussions reflect a diversity of legal traditions, perspectives and approaches, further strengthening the fairness, independence, credibility of the process and access to a fair trial.

"A court's decision can leave room for various interpretations and comments as for its legal merits; that is fair and accepted by all the judges. The court is confident in the soundness of the proceedings and the integrity of the judges. The FIA courts remain committed to the independence and impartiality of their judges and to the integrity of the judicial process."

items.title: Vuelta España Femenina to change dates from May to October for the 2027 edition
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
The women’s Vuelta España has finally set its 2027 date, with the eight-day stage race to be run between October 3 and 10, the UCI announced in a press release on Friday.

The new date not only sees the race return to its original late-season spot, but also brings the order of women’s Grand Tours into line with those on the men’s calendar.

With the men’s race pushed back, finishing in late September to accommodate the Haute-Savoie Super World Championships, the women’s race will now start the week after the men. The race also returns to the eight stage format used in 2024.

Whether the women’s race will immediately follow the men’s event from 2028 and beyond is open to question and will certainly require some juggling of the calendar. In regular seasons the World Championships begin just over a week after the men’s Vuelta concludes, but should the women’s Vuelta immediately follow the men’s race it would encroach on the Worlds, leaving no time for recovery and travel.

The Vuelta has moved around the calendar before. When it began as a one day race in 2015 it would take place on the final day of the men’s race, in early September, however, when it expanded to a full week in 2023, it moved to early May. With Itzulia Women and Vuelta Burgos Feminas held in the two following weeks, it created a cluttered spring calendar, while at the other end of the season there was very little in the way of Women’s WorldTour racing.

This season, for instance, there were only nine days of Women’s WorldTour racing after the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift, with the last European race, the Classic Lorient Agglomération, happening at the end of August and the three-day Tour of Chongming Island not taking place until October 9.

While the Vuelta España Femenina has moved, the Vuelta Burgos Feminas will take its place, the four-day race now slated to start on May 6.

These moves mitigate the lack of racing in the closing months of this year's Women's WorldTour season, creating more continuity. There will, however, be clash between the Vuelta and Chongming, which starts two days after the Spanish race, though that is a race where sprinters usually win the GC.
